Législatives en Israël : "Le 7-Octobre s’impose comme la ligne de partage de la campagne". Le cabinet du Premier ministre dénonce des accusations "totalement mensongères". L’opposition réclame des explications alors que la campagne électorale s’intensifie.

En Équateur, le secrétaire d'État américain Marco Rubio s'en prend aux cartels de la drogue. Il a annoncé que le gang équatorien Los Tiguerones serait désormais désigné comme "organisation terroriste". Biens mal acquis : deux fils de l'ex-président yéménite Ali Abdallah Saleh jugés en leur absence à Paris. Le Tchad réfute une nouvelle fois toute implication dans le conflit soudanais. N’Djaména a été accusée à de multiples reprises de servir de couloir logistique aux rebelles soudanais des Forces de soutien rapide, le gouvernement a nié systématiquement ces accusations.

L'Iran cible des navires et une base américaine en Jordanie après la destruction de pétroliers. Ceuta : La crise migratoire nourrit la désinformation. Pour leur entrée en lice en Ligue des champions, le PSG et Barcelone cartonnent. Le Rubik’s Cube, 50 ans à nous faire tourner la tête Le Hongrois Ernö Rubik (ici en 2024) n’en revient toujours pas du succès planétaire de son « invention ». - BelgaImage Il y a le rouge, le bleu, le jaune, le vert, l’orange et le blanc. Puis, après quelques rotations hasardeuses, il y a surtout le désespoir. Qui n’a jamais tenu un Rubik’s Cube entre ses mains en jurant de remettre, cette fois, chaque couleur à sa place ? Made in Budapest Son histoire commence à Budapest. En 1974, Ernö Rubik, 30 ans, est architecte et professeur. Passionné par la géométrie dans l’espace, il cherche un moyen de faire comprendre à ses étudiants comment un objet peut bouger sans perdre sa structure. Avec du bois, des élastiques et beaucoup de patience, il imagine un cube dont les différentes parties peuvent pivoter autour d’un cœur central. Puis il colore ses six faces. Le professeur vient, sans vraiment le savoir, d’inventer l’un des plus célèbres casse-tête de l’histoire. Car après avoir mélangé son prototype, Rubik se retrouve lui-même piégé. Il lui faudra plusieurs semaines pour parvenir à le remettre dans son état initial ! Des compétitions s’organisent partout, et à toutes les sauces, même les yeux bandés ! - BelgaImage En janvier 1975, il dépose une demande de brevet en Hongrie. Il faudra près de deux ans à l’administration du pays pour l’enregistrer : ce sera chose faite le 28 octobre 1976. L’objet, baptisé Büvös Kocka, le « Cube magique », peut alors commencer son incroyable aventure. Les premiers exemplaires apparaissent dans les magasins de Budapest l’année suivante. Le petit cube franchit le Rideau de fer Encore faut-il conquérir le monde. En pleine guerre froide, exporter un jouet depuis la Hongrie communiste relève presque du casse-tête dans le casse-tête. Le cube attire finalement l’attention d’hommes d’affaires occidentaux et de la société Ideal Toy. À partir de 1980, le « Magic Cube » devient le « Rubik’s Cube » et débarque à Londres, Paris et New York. Plus de 500 millions de Rubik’s Cubes ont été vendus dans le monde depuis sa création. - BelgaImage Le succès est immédiat. Dans les cours de récréation, les bureaux ou le métro, tout le monde tourne frénétiquement ses petites faces colorées. Le cube devient l’un des symboles des années 1980, au même titre que le Walkman ou Pac-Man. Des livres promettent la méthode miracle. On mémorise des suites de mouvements. En 1982, Budapest accueille le premier championnat du monde. L’Américain Minh Thai s’impose en 22,95 secondes. Un temps alors jugé presque irréel. 43 milliards de milliards de combinaisons Le secret de cette fascination tient peut-être dans un chiffre vertigineux : 43.252.003.274.489.856.000. C’est le nombre de configurations possibles d’un Rubik’s Cube classique. Plus de 43 milliards de milliards ! Et pourtant, quelle que soit la manière dont il est mélangé, il existe toujours une solution en 20 mouvements au maximum, à condition de choisir chaque déplacement parfaitement. Les mathématiciens ont surnommé cette limite le « nombre de Dieu ». Tout le génie du cube est là : un enfant comprend son but en quelques secondes, mais les mathématiques qu’il renferme peuvent occuper des chercheurs pendant des années. Le modèle classique comporte six couleurs, 54 carrés visibles et plus de 43 quintillions de combinaisons. Internet lui offre une deuxième vie Comme toutes les modes, la « Rubikmania » finit par s’essouffler. Mais le cube ne disparaît jamais vraiment. Il attend simplement son heure au fond des tiroirs. Internet va la lui offrir. À partir des années 2000, forums, tutoriels puis YouTube permettent à une nouvelle génération d’apprendre à le résoudre. Le cinéma participe au retour. Dans « À la recherche du bonheur », Will Smith impressionne son futur employeur en reconstituant un cube dans un taxi. Le Rubik’s Cube devient même une œuvre d’art. Le Français Invader utilise des centaines de cubes pour reproduire des tableaux célèbres. Sa « Rubik Mona Lisa », inspirée de La Joconde, sera adjugée plus de 480.000 euros. Le petit cube n’est décidément plus seulement un jouet. Trois secondes pour remettre le monde en ordre Aujourd’hui, il est aussi devenu un sport : le « speedcubing ». La World Cube Association organise des compétitions dans le monde entier. On y résout le cube traditionnel, mais aussi des modèles 2×2, 4×4 ou 5×5. Certaines épreuves se disputent à une main, d’autres les yeux bandés. Les chronos donnent le vertige. En 1982, Minh Thai avait été sacré en 22,95 secondes. En 2025, le Chinois Xuanyi Geng a établi un record mondial en 3,05 secondes. Et en 2026, il a encore signé une résolution en 2,80 secondes lors d’une compétition, tout en portant le record mondial de la meilleure moyenne à 3,71 secondes. Le temps de lire ce paragraphe, des meilleurs d’entre vous auraient donc déjà terminé plusieurs cubes. Le jouet qui refuse de vieillir Racheté par le groupe canadien Spin Master, le Rubik’s Cube s’est décliné sous toutes les formes : modèles géants ou miniatures, 4×4, 5×5, versions tactiles ou objets de collection. Le cube a même gagné ses galons d’objet culte. Dès 1982, le Museum of Modern Art de New York l’intègre à sa collection. Quarante ans plus tard, il continue pourtant de se vendre par millions : 5,75 millions d’exemplaires officiels ont encore trouvé preneur dans le monde en 2022. Preuve qu’à l’heure des écrans tactiles, ce petit objet que l’on manipule avec les doigts n’a rien perdu de son pouvoir d’attraction. Pourtant, l’original demeure presque inchangé. Six faces. Six couleurs. Et toujours ce petit bruit sec lorsqu’une rangée pivote. C’est peut-être là son secret. Il n’a besoin ni d’écran, ni de batterie, ni de connexion internet. Il ne parle aucune langue et tout le monde comprend immédiatement ce qu’il attend de nous : remettre un peu d’ordre dans le chaos. Cinquante ans plus tard, des centaines de millions de personnes ont essayé. Et beaucoup cherchent encore… Le Rubik’s Cube continue de nous en faire voir de toutes les couleurs. Retour sur l’incroyable destin du casse-tête le plus célèbre de la planète. Par Bertrand Deckers Le 10/09/2026 à 08:00

Prendre une année sabbatique à l’étranger : bonne ou mauvaise idée pour la suite ? Shutterstock Quel est le moment idéal pour un congé ou une année sabbatique ? Partir à l’étranger peut se faire à n’importe quel âge. On croise souvent plusieurs profils similaires. Il y a les jeunes de 18 ans qui font une année après la 6e secondaire ; il y a ceux qui sortent des études qui veulent booster leur CV et peut-être avoir une première expérience à l’étranger. Et il y a ceux qui ont commencé à travailler depuis quelques années et qui se rendent compte qu’il leur manque quelque chose et c’est souvent des compétences linguistiques. Pour eux, c’est parfois une question de prendre une pause et du temps pour soi, de rechercher du sens. Constatez-vous une augmention de ce dernier groupe ces dernières années ? Oui, c’est quelque chose qu’on remarque de plus en plus. En tout cas pour ceux qui peuvent se le permettre, car en termes de budget à prévoir, ce n’est pas négligeable. Il faut avoir des sous de côté ou une famille qui sponsorise ou qui aide. On remarque que ceux qui travaillent en ont parfois déjà marre ou se cherchent encore. Et on se dit forcément que c’est mieux de partir maintenant, quand on a 25-30 ans, plutôt que bien plus tard. Pas encore d’enfant, pas propriétaire, pas de crédit… C’est le bon moment. À l’étranger, on développe des compétences en résolution de problèmes, le courage d’affronter de nouvelles choses, de l’autonomie… Romain Hofmann Lire aussi l’article : Bosser à New York, le rêve de beaucoup de gens réalisé par Eef Au retour, comment mettre le séjour en avant sur son CV ? Ce sont des expériences qui vont être valorisées car cela montre l’ouverture vers les autres, des expériences de volontariat, des formations à l’étranger, de meilleures compétences linguistiques avec des certificats reconnus. C’est assez facile pour les recruteurs de voir qu’il y a quelque chose en plus dans ce type de profil par rapport aux autres candidats. Quelles compétences peut-on généralement acquérir lors d’un congé ou d’une année sabbatique ? Il y a la compréhension des autres, l’habitude de côtoyer des gens avec une culture différente. Quand on a vécu ailleurs, notre approche est un peu plus ouverte par rapport au travail d’équipe, à comment les gens peuvent réfléchir et ressentir les choses différemment. On développe aussi des compétences en résolution de problèmes, le courage d’affronter de nouvelles choses, l’autonomie, la débrouillardise… Étant moi-même parti, je connais le décalage courant par rapport aux amis restés en Belgique, rien que sur l’ouverture d’esprit. Quel conseil donneriez-vous à un jeune de 25-35 ans qui envisage de faire une telle pause ? Si on a déjà une hésitation, c’est qu’on se dit qu’on va le faire. En général, les raisons qui nous feraient rester en Belgique sont plutôt des peurs et des croyances. Il faut plutôt bien mettre les choses en place, préparer correctement cette période et se faire accompagner si besoin. Et puis foncer ! Quitter son emploi en début de carrière pour partir voyager ou développer ses compétences pendant des mois, voire des années de césure, est-il une bonne ou une mauvaise chose pour sa carrière ? Cinq questions à Romain Hofmann, directeur académique des programmes à long terme chez EF. Par Georges Xouras Le 10/09/2026 à 08:10 Références

Des contraceptifs augmentent le risque de développer une tumeur, 1,6 million de femmes averties en France Photo prétexte. - LESOIR Q uelque 1,6 million de femmes ayant pris un contraceptif à base de désogestrel (Antigone, Cerazette, Elfasette, Optimizette…) vont recevoir un courrier nominatif les informant d’un risque accru de développer un méningiome, annonce jeudi l’agence du médicament, jugeant toutefois ce risque « faible ». En cas de « maux de tête persistants, troubles visuels, faiblesse musculaire, troubles de l’équilibre ou du langage, perte de mémoire, ou épilepsie nouvelle ou aggravée », ces femmes doivent consulter leur médecin, indique le courrier de l’ANSM, et une imagerie cérébrale (IRM) pourra être réalisée. Car ces symptômes peuvent être dus à l’apparition d’un méningiome, une tumeur qui se développe à partir des méninges (les membranes entourant le cerveau) et qui peut causer de lourdes séquelles (vision troublée, perte auditive, d’odorat, céphalées, pertes de mémoire, crises d’épilepsie…). Toutefois, le risque pour ces femmes de développer un méningiome est très inférieur à celui lié à la prise d’Androcur, Lutényl, Lutéran, Colprone, Depo Provera, des progestatifs pour lesquels une surveillance par imagerie cérébrale est systématiquement préconisée. « Ce risque (de méningiome, NDLR) est faible, sans commune mesure avec celui de l’Androcur, qui était multiplié par 20 au bout de cinq ans », a souligné la D r Isabelle Yoldjian, directrice médicale de l’autorité sanitaire, lors d’un point presse. Dans le cas du désogestrel, une femme sur 67.000 l’ayant pris développe un méningiome lié à ce contraceptif, et une sur 17.000 à partir de cinq ans de traitement, a montré une étude du groupement d’intérêt scientifique Epi-Phare en 2024. Ce risque accru – supérieur à celui des femmes n’en ayant pas pris – est multiplié par deux au bout de sept ans de prise, mais disparaît un an après l’arrêt du contraceptif. Il concerne en particulier les femmes de plus de 45 ans et celles ayant pris auparavant un progestatif considéré comme à risque pendant plus d’un an. De leur côté, 90.000 médecins ayant prescrit une contraception à base de désogestrel seul (dosage 75 microgrammes) recevront eux aussi un courrier. L’ANSM préconise toutefois de ne pas interrompre sa contraception sans avis médical – pour ne pas risquer une grossesse non désirée – mais d’aborder ce sujet avec son médecin, sa gynécologue ou sa sage-femme lors de sa prochaine consultation de routine. Ce risque sera inscrit dans les notices de ces contraceptifs, a décidé cet été l’Agence européenne des médicaments (EMA), saisie par l’agence française du médicament. L’ANSM met aussi en ligne une « foire aux questions » (ansm.sante.fr), et rappelle que toute contraception doit être réévaluée chaque année « avec son médecin ou sa sage-femme », selon ses besoins et son état de santé. En cas de « maux de tête persistants, troubles visuels, faiblesse musculaire, troubles de l’équilibre ou du langage, perte de mémoire, ou épilepsie nouvelle ou aggravée », ces femmes doivent consulter leur médecin. لماذا قد يكون اتساخ يديك أمراً جيداً بالنسبة لك؟. اتساخ اليدين بالتراب والوحل قد لا يكون محبذاً لدى البعض، لكن العلماء يرون فيه فوائد صحية للبشرة والجهاز المناعي.
لماذا قد تكون ذكرياتنا حول 11 سبتمبر خاطئة؟. في الذكرى الخامسة والعشرين لهجمات 11 سبتمبر، نقدم لكم هذا الفيديو حول "ذكريات الوميض"، ونشرح فيه لماذا قد تكون هذه الذكريات حول الهجمات غير موثوقة تماماً.

ما هي احتمالية أن يتمكن الذكاء الاصطناعي من "قتل جميع البشر"؟. ما هي قصة أحدث حلقة في سلسلة متزايدة من التحذيرات بشأن التهديد الذي يشكّله الذكاء الاصطناعي على سلامة البشر؟

Labour party supporters also approved of the ban overwhelmingly, with 47 percent completely approving and 22 percent somewhat approving, for a total approval of 69 percent. ‘I am trapped here’: Gulf-based Nepali workers agonise as devastating floods ravage home Submitted by Areeb Ullah on Thu, 09/10/2026 - 06:24 Nepali workers in the Gulf are desperate to return home to help their loved ones but fear their employers will deny them leave or fire them from their jobs People light candles on the national day of mourning in Kathmandu on 7 September to remember the thousands of Nepalis killed in the August flash floods (Prakash Mathema/AFP) Off Under Dubai’s blinding afternoon sun, Hari Krishna lays bricks for a luxury residential complex. But his thoughts are 2,000 miles away, amid the mud and debris of Nepal’s Bhote Khosi-Trishuli corridor. For the past week, the 32-year-old construction worker, who sends most of his earnings home, has spent every spare minute frantically trying to call his relatives on iMO and checking local news channels on his cracked smartphone. Late August brought catastrophic flash floods to his home district of Nuwakot in Nepal. The waters swept away bridges, roads, and entire hillside settlements, leaving at least 1,399 people dead across the country and nearly 5,400 missing at the time of writing. And like thousands of Nepalis, the floods swept away everything Krishna’s family owned - their house, household supplies, money, gold and a shed housing their cows and goats. With their land destroyed, Krishna said there is no possibility of farming in the future. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The disaster struck his hometown in the Bidur Municipality of Nuwakot District, claiming the life of his 67-year-old grandfather. “I planned to visit my family for the upcoming Dashain festival, but that wish will now be unfulfilled with my grandfather gone,” Krishna told Middle East Eye, his voice trembling as he thought about the loss his family have experienced. “My family is sleeping in a holding centre, terrified of the next landslide, and planning my grandfather’s final death rites. Police conduct search and rescue operations in Trishuli, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, on 7 September 2026 after the flash floods in August (Pedro Pardo/AFP) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “I asked my supervisor for emergency leave, but I don’t have the money for a sudden flight, and even if I did, the roads to my village are completely washed out. “It would have been better if I was home and killed by the flood. I am trapped here.” Krishna’s plight is echoed across the Gulf, where hundreds of thousands of Nepali migrants work to support their families back home. The glittering skylines of Qatar , the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia have been built largely by South Asian labour. Now, as Nepal faces one of its most catastrophic climate disasters in recent history, the burden of rebuilding will inevitably fall on these same workers. Nepal relies heavily on its diaspora, with remittances accounting for roughly a third of its gross domestic product; remittances from the Gulf, according to the Nepal Rastra Bank, account for 40 per cent of all Nepali remittances. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); 'A systematic horror' UN agencies like the International Labour Organisation (ILO) note that extreme crises highlight how precarious the situation is for these workers. Across the migration cycle, Nepali labourers face immense risks, from their wages being withheld to limited access to healthcare. Rameshwar Nepal, an investigator for Equidem, a global human and labour rights organisation, said many Nepali workers are desperate to leave but face overwhelming logistical hurdles. “They are thousands of miles away [in the Gulf], while their families and communities face the devastation at home,” Nepal told MEE from Kathmandu, where he is coordinating relief efforts for workers and their families. “They desperately want to return home and be with their families, see if they are still alive, and see the state of their homes, properties, relatives and communities for themselves.” Damaged houses in the aftermath of the flash floods that devastated Trishuli in Nepal's Nuwakot district on 6 September 2026 (Pedro Pardo/AFP) But the journey back is laced with fear and uncertainty about whether they can return to work in the Gulf. “They don’t know whether they will be allowed to go, whether they will get paid leave, or, even if they are willing to go on unpaid leave, whether they will be allowed to do so,” Nepal explained. Beyond securing permission and covering flight costs, workers fear the long-term impact on their livelihoods. “Many of them need these jobs, particularly if they have lost their homes and property in the disaster. They need to know that they will still have a job to return to.” Nepal pointed out that the region's labour sponsorship framework exacerbates this immobility, comparing the current anxiety to the Covid-19 lockdowns. “The kafala system, which is a systematic kind of horror for migrant workers in terms of their freedom of mobility, is pertinent even in difficult situations like this,” he noted. “We saw a similar situation back in 2020... They really wanted to return to their families, but they were prevented from doing so. It sounds like a very inhuman type of situation.” 'Starting from Zero' In Qatar, 37-year-old driver Shiva Ujjwal is living that exact nightmare. Ujjwal has spent the last three years driving workers from the labour camps housing thousands of cleaners and construction workers on the outskirts of Doha to offices and building sites dotted across the Gulf capital. The driver was starting his early morning shift when disaster struck. Without a chance to check social media, he first heard the news from fellow workers. When his supervisor allowed him to use his phone, his frantic calls home failed - the communication networks in the region had been completely cut off. “My heart was breaking,” Ujjwal said, recalling the first time he saw the devastating videos online. A woman looks at photographs outside a morgue in Kathmandu on 7 September following the flash floods that swept through Nepal's Nuwakot district (Pedro Pardo/AFP) “From the scale of the flood, I could easily imagine my house had been taken away, but I was very worried about my family.” While his wife, children, and parents managed to escape safely, the human toll around them was staggering. Nine of his relatives were killed, and countless others from his village remain missing. “My family members ran with empty hands, with no chance to take important papers, money, or gold,” he explained. “We lost all our property in less than five seconds by a single hit of a live-bullet-type flood.” Burden of rebuilding For Ujjwal, who previously worked in Saudi Arabia and the UAE before moving to Qatar three years ago, the material loss represents years of erased labour. He had painstakingly built his family’s home in phases over several years, using his modest savings to fund one floor at a time. Though his Gulf wages were modest, the opportunity helped “light his kitchen” and keep his family afloat. Now, he faces the daunting prospect of starting from zero. 'We lost all our property in less than five seconds by a single hit of a live-bullet-type flood' - Shiva Ujjwal, Nepalese worker in Qatar His supervisor is arranging to send him back to Nepal on unpaid leave, but the geographic and emotional distance has taken a heavy toll, especially during the initial multi-day communication blackout. “It is very stressful to stay here as my family is in a holding centre now,” he said, burdened by the thought of how to eventually rebuild their home. “My body is here, but I am not here.” For the Nepali diaspora in the Gulf, the immediate response has been mobilisation. Grassroots fundraising campaigns are circulating through WhatsApp groups as workers pool their meagre savings to send bulk relief to the hardest-hit districts. Yet, for men like Ujjwal and Krishna, the financial support feels like a hollow substitute for being home. Yemen rebels report fresh Saudi strikes as conflict deepens. Yemen’s Houthi rebels reported dozens of Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday as daily attacks continued in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war, with hundreds of people killed in fighting near the Red Sea. More than 40 attacks targeted several regions, including the flashpoint areas of Taiz and Hodeida, the scene of fierce clashes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition government, the rebels said. The latest salvos in Yemen’s previously dormant conflict come a day after the Houthis set oil sites ablaze and wounded 73 in their heaviest missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia in years. The fighting in Yemen is taking place against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which erupted in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran. On Wednesday, Iran said it attacked 20 American vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and targeted a US military base in Jordan in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian oil tankers. The Middle East war has sucked in Yemen, the energy-rich Gulf and others across the region while roiling the world economy, as oil prices returned to $100 a barrel on Wednesday. More than 500 people have died since the Houthis launched a major offensive last week to seize territory around the Bab al-Mandab strait, gateway to the Red Sea shipping route. This frame grab taken from AFPTV video footage on September 9, shows smoke billowing during clashes between Yemeni government forces and Houthi fighters in the Al-Kadha area, west of Taiz province, on September 8. — AFP The rebels, who have been attacking Saudi oil tankers, are trying to tighten their squeeze on the shipments, which analysts say are a lifeline for exports after the blockade of Hormuz. ‘Dangerous escalation’ Saudi airstrikes targeted “various areas across the governorates of Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeida over the past few hours”, the rebels’ Almasirah TV said on Wednesday. There was no official comment from Saudi Arabia. The Saudi civil defence later issued a warning for the southern governorate of Khamis Mushait, near Yemen, but quickly lifted it. On Tuesday, Saudi authorities vowed to respond to the Houthi attacks, saying they caused fires and temporary shutdowns at oil sites. This frame grab taken on September 9, 2026, from video footage released by the Saudi Ministry of Media on September 8, 2026, shows damage following Houthi strikes at an undisclosed location in southern Saudi Arabia. — AFP The Houthis triggered the return to hostilities in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace. The government retaliated by striking the airport, an attack the rebels blamed on Saudi Arabia. The ongoing exchanges risk returning Yemen to a conflict that left hundreds of thousands of people dead and sparked one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The Houthis, after seizing Yemen’s capital and forcing out the internationally recognised government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022. On Tuesday, the European Union urged the Houthis to end their attacks, calling them a “dangerous escalation”. “We call on the Houthis to immediately end all attacks inside and outside Yemen, including attacks against commercial shipping in the Red Sea,” said Anouar El Anouni, a spokesman for the bloc’s diplomatic service.

Asif warns Makkah defence pact could become operational after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has cautioned that the tripartite Makkah Defence Alliance between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye could become operational if there was a “spillover” of the conflict in Yemen into Riyadh. The development comes after Yemen’s Houthi rebels launched attacks on oil installations in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, injuring 73 people. Meanwhile, the defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. On the Geo News show ‘ Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath ’ on Tuesday night, host Shahzeb Khanzada mentioned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and asked Asif whether the strategic pact could be operationalised. Asif answered in the affirmative, saying there was no “ambiguity” as the pact stipulated that aggression against one party was equivalent to aggression against all. “This is a joint defence pact. And unprovoked aggression or spillover of whatever is happening in Yemen into Saudi Arabia, definitely, the pact will become operational; there should be no doubt in this,” he said. “We are bound by the terms and conditions of this pact and we will honour them in case there is a need,” he said. Asked if Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had been in contact following the attacks, Asif said he was not aware of any engagement. However, he reiterated that Pakistan “is bound to react under the pact because it is [aimed at] joint defence and collective help in case of aggression”. Asif further stated that the pact was not “aggressive in nature”, adding: “If there is aggression against one member state, then all three member states will respond in kind.” The defence czar went on to say, “This is a trilateral pact [..] but even if it were bilateral, we would have responded.” At the same time, Asif expressed hope that the situation will “come under control and die down”. He also hoped that “the Houthis will realise that if [..] they attempt to export their internal matters, then the clauses of this pact over confronting aggression will become operative”. “They should keep this in mind,” he said. Asif also noted that the Houthis were “non-state actors” and that Yemen’s government had responded to their attacks. “There is sympathy for Iran around the Muslim world. There is no doubt about that, but exploitation of a bilateral dispute by non-state actors, I believe they are doing it at their own peril,” he said. Asif observed that the pact could serve as a deterrent and went on to say that three countries “did not need to respond to aggression with aggression”, but held that the member states had established their respective strengths. The defence minister added that the conflict in Yemen had been ongoing since 2014, recalling a visit he made to the country at the time in his capacity as the defence minister. “At that time too, we helped Saudi Arabia,” he recalled, adding that Pakistan and Saudi’s long-standing ties and the “sanctity” of the Gulf country’s land “warrant that whenever there are testing times, we help them”. On the stalemate in negotiations between the United States and Iran, the defence minister voiced optimism that “all doors have not closed”. “I will not abandon hope that the process has ended or that all doors have closed. There is a stalemate, but I will say the situation is better than that,” he said, adding there was “indirect engagement”. He noted that Pakistan walked a tightrope given its “brotherly relations” with countries on both sides of the conflict. Hoping that peace would prevail, Asif warned: “Israel will want that the conflict should continue and (Gulf) countries should be drained.” He said Israel was not incurring any expenses in the war, as the funding “was coming from overseas”. “In fact, I believe they are profiting off of it,” he said. He noted that people in Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon were paying the price for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s “lust for power”. However, he went on to note that there was a “silver lining”. “In the world over, especially Europe, North America, New Zealand, Latin America, there is a sea [of] change in the opinions of people and people want to get rid of the Zionist lobby,” he said. On Tuesday, the rebel group claimed attacks on four cities in the south of Saudi Arabia, which wounded more than 70 people and set oil installations ablaze. The Houthis said they had fired dozens of ballistic missiles, hitting the southern cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan, and Najran, including Abha International Airport, King Khalid air base, and facilities belonging to state oil giant Aramco. In response, Saudi Arabia retaliated with strikes on Taiz and Marib provinces, as well as the Jubah district, east of the capital Sanaa. At the time, the Saudi foreign ministry said Riyadh would “take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty”. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had condemned the Houthi attack and assured Saudi Arabia of Pakistan’s “unwavering solidarity”. “Such dastardly attacks threaten innocent lives as well as regional peace and security. We reaffirm our steadfast support for the kingdom’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity, and pray for the swift recovery of all those injured,” he said in a post on X. The Foreign Office also issued a statement condemning the “reprehensible” attacks.

Islamabad admin announces 'complete ban' on sheesha cafes as IHC gives a month to formulate regulations. ISLAMABAD: Islamabad Deputy Commissioner (DC) Irfan Nawaz Memon on Wednesday announced a “complete” ban on running sheesha cafes in the federal capital. “Immediately implementing the Islamabad High Court’s order, a complete ban has been imposed on running sheesha cafes in the federal capital until further orders,” the DC posted on X. He added that the restriction also covered all kinds of sheesha cafes, including those that had no-objection certificates (NOCs) and outdoor and indoor cafes. Cafes found in violation of the order would be sealed, and a case would be registered against the owner, he warned, adding that assistant commissioners would ensure inspections on a daily basis. The DC’s announcement came after the Islamabad High Court (IHC) observed earlier in the day that sheesha cafes couldn’t be allowed to operate without a proper regulatory framework and gave the district administration one month to formulate comprehensive rules and regulations. IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar issued the directive while hearing petitions pertaining to several sheesha cafes in Islamabad and the action taken against establishments that had been allegedly operating in violation of their NOCs, issued under an interim arrangement. DC Memon and Islamabad Inspector General of Police (IG) Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi also appeared before the court in their personal capacities at the hearing. Islamabad Advocate General Naveed Hayat Malik and acting Prosecutor General Manzoor Ahmed Jajja were also present. During the proceedings, the chief justice said that the court respected the business interests of cafe owners, but the entire city could not be allowed to be affected in the name of business. “Tomorrow, your brother or someone from your family could become a victim,” the chief justice remarked, referring to health implications. He questioned the manner in which sheesha was being served, observing that if hashish was mixed with tobacco, it would amount to smoking. He further remarked that such activities were taking place openly and warned that the younger generation was being pushed towards destruction. The Islamabad police chief informed the court that strict action had been taken against sheesha cafes following the court’s earlier directives, and cases had been registered against some establishments. The IG claimed that police teams had faced resistance from cafe owners during raids and that children aged 14 and 15 had also been found at some establishments. He further stated that an awareness campaign regarding the harmful effects and regulation of sheesha cafes had also been launched. Following that, CJ Dogar observed that sheesha cafes could not be allowed to operate as they were running presently, without rules and regulations. “There are no rules and regulations,” the chief justice observed, adding that the existing arrangement was damaging the lives of people in Islamabad. Acting Prosecutor General Jajja told the court that children aged 18 or below were among those involved in selling sheesha and suggested that directions be issued to the Ministry of Health and the federal government to formulate proper rules. He said the issue was more serious than that of smog and required a comprehensive regulatory response. When the CJ asked whether the cafe owners “shut their doors” when a police team conducted raids, the Islamabad IG replied in the affirmative, saying that it had been several times. During the proceedings, the chief commissioner and district administration submitted their written response to the court. According to the response, NOCs for sheesha cafes are currently being issued under an interim arrangement pending approval of regular legislation by the federal government. The district administration said all NOCs had been issued without any fee. The response stated separate standard operating procedures (SOPs) were not considered necessary as the criteria for issuing NOCs were based on the high court’s directives and World Health Organisation’s guidelines (WHO). Under the existing arrangement, sheesha could only be served in an open, unroofed area. A separate written “terrace permit” was required from the assistant commissioner concerned for serving sheesha at an open-air location, the response said. The assistant commissioner concerned would be given the authority to inspect an establishment, impose additional conditions and take action according to law upon receiving complaints from the public, it added. The administration said a crackdown against sheesha cafes in Islamabad had been launched in 2021 and that unsafe storage of coal and related equipment posed a significant fire hazard. It added that fire prevention and safety measures had been made mandatory for restaurants, while inspection teams had also been directed to check the validity and safety of fire extinguishers. The administration maintained that sheesha and other tobacco products could only be served to adults and that environmental standards were required to be maintained. It further stressed the need to implement international and legal regulations to protect citizens from exposure to tobacco smoke. For its part, the IHC said that the existing court-approved arrangement would remain in force until the federal government framed regular rules. He directed the district administration to formulate the required rules within one month and adjourned the hearing.

Two navy personnel martyred while patrolling at sea: DGPR. Two Pakistan Navy personnel were martyred while patrolling at sea to ensure security, the Navy’s Directorate-General of Public Relations (DGPR) said on Wednesday. “Shoaibur Rehman (PMA-IV) and Ghufran Nasar (PMT-II) embraced martyrdom while performing patrolling duties at sea to ensure security,” it said in a statement on X. As per the statement, Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf expressed deep sorrow over the loss of precious lives. “Senior Pakistan Navy officials attended the funerals of martyred sailors and met their families,” it added. In March this year, the Pakistan Navy had launched Operation Muhafizul Bahr to counter “multidimensional threats to national shipping and maritime trade”. According to the Pakistan Navy, the decision — which followed the launch of the US-Iran war — was made in light of the “evolving regional maritime security environment and potential disruptions to critical sea lanes”. The statement noted that with approximately 90 per cent of Pakistan’s trade conducted via sea, the operation aimed to ensure that vital sea routes remained safe, secure, and uninterrupted.

PML-N, ANP senators spar over death of Gujranwala sanitary worker at Senate committee meeting. ISLAMABAD: A meeting of the Senate Functional Committee on Human Rights turned acrimonious on Wednesday as PML-N Senator Abid Sher Ali and ANP chief Senator Aimal Wali Khan clashed over the questioning of Suthra Punjab officials in connection with the death of a Gujranwala waste management worker. Chaired by Senator Samina Mumtaz Zehri, the committee was reviewing the death of an employee of the Gujranwala Waste Management Company (GWMC), who allegedly died by suicide after receiving half his salary and facing termination of his contract. Tensions rose when Senator Khan pressed officials with pointed questions. Senator Ali interrupted, objecting to the tone. “Listen to them — you are conducting an inquiry and asking questions as if you are sitting in a police station,” he said. When a member suggested that the cameras be switched off, Ali said he had “nothing wrong to say”. “Speak properly,” he told Khan. “I am speaking properly — you speak properly too,” Khan shot back. Senators, including Qurratulain Marri, intervened to defuse the situation. Officials told the committee that the worker had been with GWMC from 2024 to 2025 and that his contract had expired on May 31. The alleged suicide, they said, occurred after his employment had ended. Khan alleged that the worker had been paid only half his salary. “A common labourer was pushed to the point where he took his own life,” he said. The GWMC CEO disputed this, saying bank records showed full salary payments and that the worker had performance issues. Committee members questioned why Suthra Punjab was engaging a third party for cleaning staff instead of recruiting workers directly. Senator Marri pointed out that the Suthra Punjab Act came into force in 2026, while the incident took place in 2025. “How was recruitment done before the institution formally existed?” she asked. Khan echoed the concern. The CEO said the sanitary worker had initially been engaged in 2025 through a contractor and was later rehired and deputed to the IT room of the Suthra Punjab office as a naib qasid. He was later dismissed on grounds of misconduct, the committee was told. The GWMC CEO said compensation had been provided to the worker’s widow and children, including a plot purchased with the help of a chamber of commerce. When Senator Khan asked why a plot had been given if the worker was not in service, he remarked: “If you give me a plot too, I will also be happy.” Officials suggested the worker may have had personal problems. The ANP chief rejected the claim, saying: “You casually made an allegation that there was a love affair involved in why he died.” The committee directed Suthra Punjab to submit all relevant documents and copies of the laws for 2025 and 2026 and asked whether any redressal mechanism existed beyond financial compensation. The chairperson directed that the deceased’s family be invited to the next meeting to present their position. On July 1, a Suthra Punjab worker set himself on fire in Gujranwala in protest against non-payment of his full salary. He succumbed to his injuries two days later. A CCTV camera recorded footage of the employee when he was coming out of the office where he had gone to complain against the contractor, later showing him dowsing himself in petrol in the corridor in the presence of some staff members. Some other employees present there rushed to save their colleague and threw water on him, the CCTV footage showed. An official said the contractor had been illegally deducting a major chunk of the workers’ Rs21,000 monthly salary. On July 17, the Senate Functional Committee on Human Rights expressed concern over the worker’s alleged suicide. It sought complete records, including contracts, salary registers, tax documents and banking transactions, to examine possible violations. It also directed authorities to provide details of compensation and insurance for the deceased worker’s family. Other cases taken up The Additional IG Sindh briefed the committee on the case of Mir Raza. His father had reported him missing in July 2026. The first post-mortem was conducted on July 30, and a second was conducted at the request of the accused’s family. Senator Ali questioned the need for a second autopsy. The committee was told that the SHO had failed to preserve the crime scene and had shifted the body to the hospital. Both the SHO and DSP were suspended for negligence. The committee recommended the arrest of the SHO. On the Jaranwala incident of August 16, 2023, officials said 389 people had been arrested and several cases were under trial or had been concluded. Expressing concern over delays, the chairperson said the matter involved a minority community and required urgent resolution. Senator Ali stressed the need for justice and adequate compensation. The Chief Secretary’s representative said an assessment committee would evaluate losses with community representatives and that Rs2 million would be given to each affected family. The families, however, said the amount did not match their actual losses. The chairperson directed that compensation be determined on the basis of actual damages. The committee also reviewed the target killing of Ahmed Javed. It was told that the main accused, who was out on bail, was appearing in court with 40-50 people, allegedly intimidating witnesses. The committee recommended applying to the court to stop the practice. Senator Khan criticised the working of the CCD in Punjab and CTD in KP. The chairperson also questioned the NCCIA’s performance regarding alleged malicious social media material uploaded by the accused.

FATF warns of emerging risks to economies from rising online gaming, gambling operations. ISLAMABAD: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) has warned of emerging risks to economies from rising online gaming and gambling operations, while sharing new risk indicators with countries to combat money laundering and terror financing. “As gaming and gambling services become increasingly digital, cross-border and interconnected, new money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing risks are emerging,” said the FATF, the Paris-based global watchdog on money laundering, terror financing and proliferation financing related to weapons of mass destruction, on Wednesday after conducting surveys across 80 jurisdictions. The findings and risk indicators examine risks across casinos, gambling and online gaming, including online platforms, payment channels, illegal operators and their links to the broader financial system. The FATF said it also sets international standards to combat illicit finance and assesses whether countries are taking effective action. The latest report said the gaming and gambling industries had changed significantly in recent years and continued to evolve through the expansion of online, cross-border, multi-product and multi-payment platforms. “Gaming and gambling establishments and platforms are now part of a broader interconnected value transfer ecosystem with numerous actors, some of which fall outside national anti-money laundering/counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT) regulatory frameworks,” it said. These factors, as well as the varying scope among jurisdictions in AML/CFT regulation of gambling and understanding of gaming risk-exposed activity, have led to developments in the money laundering (ML), terrorist financing (TF) and, to a somewhat lesser extent, proliferation financing (PF) risks associated with the sector. The FATF also alerted countries and regulators to ways of spotting and blocking the abuse of the gaming and gambling sectors, including criminals using gambling platforms to move money without actually gambling, making multiple small transactions (“smurfing”) to avoid detection, and placing unusually large or coordinated bets on events flagged for possible competition manipulation. Analysis by the FATF identified new opportunities for criminal abuse in the gaming and gambling sectors, following an increase in the global market size, a rise in the use of online platforms and the growing use of payment methods that allow rapid, anonymous transactions across borders. It identified illegal gambling as one of the sector’s most significant risks. In many jurisdictions, illegal markets rival or even exceed the size of legal gambling markets. Illegal gambling operators are prevalent across jurisdictions, regardless of the legal status of gambling or the regulatory frameworks in place. Illegal and unlicensed offshore operators often present themselves as legitimate businesses while offering anonymity and incentives that can attract both consumers and criminal actors. It said technological innovation had expanded activity across online, cross-border and multi-payment platforms, creating increasingly complex ecosystems for regulators and law enforcement. With gaming and gambling activities increasingly interconnected with the wider digital economy, the sector provides multiple points of access to the formal financial system through cash, e-wallets, mobile money and virtual assets. Gaming and gambling platforms depend on a wide range of related services, including social media platforms, digital marketplaces and software developers. These actors may fall outside existing regulatory frameworks, creating additional opportunities for criminal abuse. It warned that criminals and illegal operators can exploit differences in regulatory approaches across jurisdictions. These differences can also create barriers to information sharing between the private and public sectors and pose challenges to international cooperation. The FATF also warned that beneficial ownership and shareholding structures of platforms can be designed to bypass thresholds for regulatory checks, especially when AML/CFT controls and anti-corruption frameworks are weak. FATF President Giles Thomson urged governments to take note of the risk indicators and put in place appropriate risk-based responses — from strengthening oversight and cracking down on illegal and offshore operators to boosting international cooperation and deepening public-private collaboration. It also highlighted the continued threat of criminal infiltration and exploitation of gaming and gambling operators and identified links between gaming and gambling abuse and a range of other offences, including corruption, cyber-enabled fraud, professional money laundering networks, and the use of illegal or unlicensed offshore operators to facilitate criminal activity. The new risk indicators also provide practical guidance to identify, assess and respond to suspicious activity. The indicators highlight behavioural, transactional and operational warning signs associated with money laundering and terrorist financing. These include the use of multiple accounts and payment methods under different identities, discrepancies between customer and payment information, suspicious identity documents and criminal links involving gambling operators or beneficial owners, including involvement in cyber-enabled fraud and organised crime; suspicious betting and transaction patterns; and complex ownership structures that obscure beneficial ownership. Regulators have been alerted to be vigilant for attempts to influence or bribe venue staff through frequent dealings with one or two staff members, requests for cash-ups, claims through lottery tickets, betting slips, vouchers or prize coupons, and taking instructions from customers over a mobile phone. Warning signs also include deliberate attempts to conceal identity, such as repeated use of virtual private networks (VPNs), use of multiple devices and discrepancies between a customer’s claimed residence and their detected location. Customers may also try to open multiple accounts under the same name or a false name, while an internet protocol (IP) address may not match the customer’s stated location.

Pakistan among Arab, Muslim nations welcoming UK ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Pakistan, along with seven other Arab and Muslim countries, on Wednesday welcomed the United Kingdom’s decision to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. UK imposed the trade measures on Tuesday, alongside Canada and France. The decision was announced by British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who accused the Israeli government of turning a “blind eye” to what he called “ethnic cleansing” by settlers in the West Bank. Meanwhile, a joint statement by the foreign ministers of 12 nations, including Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden, also expressed an intention to follow suit and stressed that the Israeli government’s actions in the West Bank undermined the possibility of a two-state solution. A joint statement by the foreign ministers of Pakistan, Turkiye, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, issued by the Foreign Office (FO), expressed hope that the international community would take similar action in accordance with international law and “hold accountable settlement organisations and individuals engaged in illegal settlement activities”. The ministers also welcomed an earlier joint statement on the two-state solution issued by the foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. “They encourage the international community to build on these steps and adopt concrete measures to bring an end to activities that support or sustain illegal Israeli settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory,” the FO stated. It added that the eight countries considered the ban to be in line with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions, including Security Council Resolution 2334 (2016). They also viewed the decision as consistent with the International Court of Justice’s July 19, 2024, advisory opinion, which requires states “not to recognise as legal the situation arising from Israel’s unlawful occupation and not to render aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by Israel’s occupation”. “In this regard, they reiterate their call for Israel to rescind all measures taken in connection with settlement activities and other measures aimed at altering the geographic and demographic character of the Occupied Palestinian Territory,” the joint statement read. The joint statement also stressed that Gaza is an integral part of Palestine and called for the “full and immediate” implementation of US President Donald Trump’s ‘Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict’. The ministers reiterated that the only viable path to a lasting and comprehensive peace was the implementation of a two-state solution and the establishment of an independent, sovereign, contiguous and viable Palestinian state based on the June 4, 1967, borders, with Jerusalem as its capital, in accordance with international law. Islamabad stands by Palestine Earlier today, Pakistan welcomed the United Kingdom-led decision to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, saying that the illegal settlements undermined efforts towards a two-state solution, a separate statement from the FO read. In a statement on its X account, the FO welcomed the decision and said: “The continued expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory constitutes a blatant violation of international law as well as relevant UN Security Council resolutions.” Maintaining that Israel’s actions were a hindrance to a two-state solution, the FO also welcomed the joint statement by the 12 countries, which it said were considering “similar measures and support[ing] such efforts against the illegal Israeli settlements”. “Pakistan hopes that these measures will send a clear and unequivocal message of rejection of illegal actions in the occupied Palestinian territory,” the statement said. Islamabad reiterated support for Palestine, vowing to stand by its people and “their just struggle for self-determination”. In response to the UK’s actions, Israel ordered the closure of the UK’s consulate in Jerusalem earlier today. It also said it would expel British representatives at a centre monitoring the US-brokered ceasefire plan in Gaza, bar British training for Palestinian Authority forces and ban 12 Britons, mostly members of parliament, from visiting the country. Miliband, in response, condemned Israel’s actions as “regrettable and damaging”. Speaking to BBC Radio , he also rejected suggestions that the sanctions would impact intelligence cooperation with Israel. “We have important intelligence and security relationships with Israel, and I’m confident they will continue,” he said, declining to go into details. “And I was very clear yesterday that we do believe in working with our Israeli partners when it comes to the threats they face from Iran,” he added.

Pakistan’s UN envoy Asim Iftikhar named new foreign secretary. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Wednesday announced the appointment of Pakistan’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, as the country’s new foreign secretary. “I am delighted to also announce that Ambassador Ahmad, who is currently Pakistan’s permanent representative to the UN, will be the next Foreign Secretary of Pakistan,” FM Dar said in a post on X. “I am confident that, under Ambassador Iftikhar’s leadership, the Foreign Office will continue to advance Pakistan’s interests with clarity, professionalism and purpose, building on the important work undertaken by Ambassador Amna Baloch and all her predecessors,” he added. Moreover, FM Dar commended Amna Baloch, the current foreign secretary, for her “dedicated service and leadership of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs during a consequential period in Pakistan’s diplomatic history”. “Baloch leaves behind a legacy of dedicated public service and carries with her our warmest wishes,” he stated. FM Dar said that Baloch would assume charge as Pakistan’s ambassador to Türkiye after her retirement. “I am confident she will continue to serve Pakistan with distinction in this new role,” he said. According to the foreign minister, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had also approved the aforementioned assignments. Baloch has been serving as Pakistan’s 33rd foreign secretary since September 11, 2024. She will retire from government service on September 17. In a post on X, Ambassador Ahmad also hailed his appointment as “a great honour”. “Deeply humbled by the confidence and trust reposed by the leadership. Looking forward to carrying out together this responsibility in advancing supreme national interest,” he said. “Thankful to Allah for His blessings, and to parents, family, friends and colleagues for their support and prayers.”

Tongue routs Pakistan as England dominate in third Test. England are on course to complete a series whitewash after Pakistan’s brittle batting collapsed again on the opening day of the third Test at Edgbaston on Wednesday. The tourists, who have failed to reach 200 in the series, were dismantled once more by England’s four-man pace attack and were shot out for 133 in just 33.5 overs. Josh Tongue led the way with 4-42 with Ollie Robinson taking 3-15 and Jofra Archer 3-25. Debutant Razaullah enjoyed a dream start to his Pakistan test career, taking the prize wicket of Joe Root with his fourth ball, but a century stand from Emilio Gay and Harry Brook put England in command. They closed with a lead of 23 on 156-4. Razaullah, 21, was one of three new caps, along with wicketkeeper Ghazi Ghori and Mohammad Imran, in a Pakistan side thrown into chaos when seven players were sent home after the second test loss at Lords. Coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and his assistant Umar Gul were also sacked in the aftermath. The pattern of the series was maintained with Pakistan getting away to another awful start after being put in to bat, slumping to 26-4 inside the opening hour. Saim Ayub, recalled after a 21-month absence, was trapped lbw by Robinson, giving the Sussex captain his 100th Test wicket in his 24th test, and opening partner Azan Awais was caught by a diving Tongue at wide mid-on off Archer for nine. Abdullah Shafique followed, caught well low down to his left at gully by Dan Lawrence off Robinson for three. When Shan Masood miscued a pull to mid-on off Archer, the tourists were reeling. Pakistan’s problems mounted when Tongue was introduced. He bowled Pakistan captain Babar Azam in his first over for seven, trapped Ghazi for four before yorking Imran for five. At lunch Pakistan were in disarray at 100-7. Razaullah lasted just three balls after the resumption, edging Robinson to Ben Duckett who made amends for two earlier spills with the catch. Saud Shakeel, who hit 97 at Lords, top-scored again with 43 from 47 balls before becoming Tongue’s fourth victim. It said much about Pakistan’s limp effort that the highest partnership of the innings was the last-wicket stand of 26 between Mohammad Abbas, who made 21, and Mohammad Ali. England did not have it all their own way when their turn came on a surface offering some help to the bowlers with Ali and Abbas nipping out Duckett and Jordan Cox respectively early on. When Root fell lbw for the ninth time in his last 12 test innings, England were 39-3 but Brook and Gay restored order. For Gay, still establishing himself in the England side, his highest Test score of 60 from 114 balls was an important contribution. He exited late on, dragging on a ball from the impressive Razaullah, who touched 90mph, but Brook will be at the crease on 52 tomorrow morning alongside Lawrence.

Republicans put Trump centre stage in US midterms gamble. US Republicans open an extraordinary midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, betting that putting Donald Trump at the centre of their campaign can rescue a party facing grim election forecasts — despite the president’s deeply negative approval ratings. The two-day gathering, dubbed “Trumpapalooza,” is designed to persuade the Republican leader’s supporters that he is effectively on the ballot on November 3, when Republicans risk losing the House of Representatives and face a fierce fight to retain the Senate. “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said recently at a rally in South Carolina. “Just come and vote. It’s so important.” Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House 230-205 and the Senate to finish 51-49 in their favour — revising its 50-50 prediction as the outlook continues to worsen for Republicans. Trump, whose approval rating stood at just 33 per cent in recent polling , will speak on both convention nights at the American Airlines Centre. U.S. President Donald Trump walks to board Marine One, en route to Dallas, Texas, at the Ellipse near the White House in Washington, DC, the US on September 9, 2026. — Reuters His challenge is to mobilise voters personally loyal to him without further alienating independents already souring on his presidency amid inflation woes, gasoline prices topping $4 a gallon and the continuing war on Iran . “Many Trump supporters only vote when he’s on the ballot,” Matthew Green, a politics professor at the Catholic University of America, told AFP . “They’re not diehard Republican voters; they’re diehard Trump voters. So, in that respect, it makes some sense to feature Trump in the hopes of getting those folks to turn out in November.” But Green was sceptical that asking those supporters to imagine Trump on their ballots could overcome his broader weakness. “When you’re in the low- to mid-30s, that’s traditionally associated with a very bad midterm for your party,” he said of the 80-year-old’s approval ratings. Trump show The gathering is the first Republican national convention held specifically for a midterm election, although no candidates will be nominated and no formal party business is planned. Instead, organisers have constructed what amounts to a two-night television rally touting Trump’s record and Republican candidates. More than 100 House members and candidates are expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night. Rubber ducks shaped as US President Donald Trump are seen at a store outside of the American Airlines Centre ahead of the 2026 Republican National Committee (RNC) Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas on September 08, 2026. — AFP Trump delivers Wednesday’s keynote and returns for Thursday’s finale after Vice President JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the program. Republicans plan to highlight tax cuts, immigration enforcement, manufacturing and prescription drug prices, while depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left. Some Republicans, however, are privately hoping Trump sticks to that script rather than the personal grievances and off-message subjects that regularly dominate his appearances. Staying home Not everyone is coming. Numerous lawmakers in competitive races have decided that, less than two months from Election Day, their time is better spent campaigning at home. House Speaker Mike Johnson has acknowledged the dilemma, saying some members need to remain home because it is a “critical time” immediately before early voting accelerates nationwide. And even Trump’s promised national television showcase faces an unusually formidable rival. Both convention nights coincide with the opening games of the NFL season. “Spending three or four days away from your district to go to a convention is not a good way to spend your time if you’re facing a tight re-election,” Green added. Democrats were also making their presence felt in Dallas, with the party sending out some of its most high-profile speakers for public events. “Americans are being crushed by rising costs,” Colorado Congressman Jason Crow posted on X. “Republicans don’t care — they’re in Dallas, celebrating an out-of-touch President whose tariffs and wars are making things worse. We’re going to hold them accountable.”

Goods transport owners demand release of containers seized by Islamabad police. ISLAMABAD: Goods transporters on Wednesday demanded that the Ministry of Interior release containers detained by Islamabad police ahead of the PTI’s scheduled Islamabad long march at the end of the month. The PTI, with the confidence and support of the opposition alliance — Tehreek-i-Tahaffuz Ayeen-i-Pakistan (TTAP) — has announced a long march towards Islamabad against what it calls the “illegal” detention of party founder and ex-premier Imran Khan and to demand his release. The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Tuesday decided to form a larger bench to hear a petition against the PTI’s planned protest, terming the matter sensitive and observing that it could have constitutional implications. In a statement on Wednesday, All Pakistan Goods Transport Owners Association President Muhammad Owais Chaudhry expressed concern over the seizure of container vehicles by Islamabad police, saying that the vehicles and containers should not be used for political purposes or to block roads during possible political activity on September 27. He said that around 100 container vehicles had been taken into custody from different areas of Islamabad, mainly Sangjani and Tarnol, the statement said. “The containers were being kept to possibly to block roads during the anticipated protest.” “What we demand is that there are a large number of containers available for rent in and around the federal capital — the Islamabad police or the administration should rent empty containers and use them as they wish,” Chaudhry was quoted as saying. He added that some impounded vehicles had reportedly been parked in deserted areas, while containers had allegedly been removed from certain vehicles, causing financial losses and business difficulties for their owners. “We had to facilitate the transporters in removing the goods from the containers — because the authorities do not take responsibility for the loss or damage to the cargo,” he added. Meanwhile, the association said it had received complaints from transporters alleging that some seized vehicles and containers were released after money was paid, while several others remained in police custody. It demanded a transparent investigation into the allegations and said the transporters had political affiliations on an individual basis. Their opposition to the impounding of vehicles, it added, should not be construed as a political link with the PTI, as the commercial vehicles were meant for trade and economic activity, “not for safety and security purposes of the police department”. The association also warned the government against impounding the vehicles, saying their forced use for political purposes created “an impression of state coercion”.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs367.75 per litre while HSD will cost Rs392.67 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable on Sept 10 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. On July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

PM to highlight efforts to end US-Iran war at UNGA. • Bangladesh assumes presidency as General Assembly formally opens in New York • Trump to speak on opening day; PM Shehbaz’s speech on 25th; Pezeshkian’s attendance ‘not yet confirmed’ • Renewal on the cards as tenure of panel monitoring Iran sanctions expires during UNGA session WASHINGTON: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is due to arrive in New York later this month for the UN General Assembly, where he is expected to highlight Pakistan’s efforts to find a peaceful solution to the ongoing US-Iran war. PM Shehbaz is slated to address the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 25, where the Gulf conflict is expected to overshadow much of the high-level debate. The official theme of the 81st session is ‘Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All’, and the UNGA debate is expected to run from Sept 22 to 26, with a final sitting on Sept 28. However, ongoing fighting between Washington and Tehran is expected to feature prominently in discussions among world leaders, particularly over the security of the Strait of Hormuz, regional stability and the possibility of finding a diplomatic way out of the confrontation. The participation of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is also emerging as a key question ahead of the high-level week. Iran is listed on the tentative speakers’ schedule as the fifth speaker on Sept 23, the second day of the UNGA debate, but a final decision on whether he will travel to New York or not, has not yet been made. Iranian officials have indicated that Tehran is still assessing the level of participation and attendance, citing what they describe as “illegal conditions” imposed by Washington on the Iranian delegation’s travel and attendance. US President Donald Trump is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Sept 22, the opening day of the high-level debate, following Brazil, which traditionally opens the general debate. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is also expected to attend reception hosted by President Trump on the same day. Israel, the other party to the conflict, is scheduled to speak on Sept 24, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu representing his country. India, meanwhile, is only sending its foreign minister, who is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Sept 26. According to diplomatic sources, Pakistan is expected to use the forum of the UN General Assembly to underline its position that the conflict should be resolved through negotiations rather than prolonged military confrontation. The prime minister is also expected to highlight Islamabad’s contacts with countries involved in efforts to de-escalate the situation. The Iranian issue is already occupying a prominent place on the UN agenda ahead of the arrival of world leaders. The Security Council is scheduled to vote on Sept 17 on renewing the mandate of the panel of experts monitoring sanctions on Iran. The panel’s mandate expires on Sept 26, during the General Assembly’s high-level week. The proposed renewal is expected to produce another confrontation between the United States and its Western allies on one side and Russia and China on the other. Moscow and Beijing have opposed continuation of the monitoring mechanism, arguing that the Security Council no longer has the authority to pursue the matter in its present form. The dispute is linked to the restoration of UN sanctions on Iran under the “snapback” mechanism after Britain, France and Germany concluded last year that Tehran was not complying with its obligations under the 2015 nuclear agreement. Iran has rejected allegations that it is seeking nuclear weapons. The Sept 17 vote will therefore come just days before heads of government begin arriving for the General Assembly and could further sharpen the diplomatic divisions surrounding Iran. For Pakistan, the situation carries additional urgency because of its geographical proximity to the conflict and its economic and security interests in the Gulf region. The prime minister will be accompanied by a high-level delegation, including senior members of the government, and is expected to hold a series of bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the General Assembly. The UN session formally opened on Wednesday, with Bangladesh’s Khalilur Rahman assuming the presidency of the 81st General Assembly. Mr Rahman has placed peace and security, restoration of trust in multilateral institutions and UN reform among the priorities of his presidency. The session also comes ahead of a major change in the UN hierarchy, as it would be the last for current Secretary General Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on Dec 31, 2026. Published in Dawn, September 10th, 2026

New provinces not only way to improve governance: Gohar. PESHAWAR: Calling for caution in decisions regarding the creation of new provinces , PTI Interim Chairman Barri­ster Gohar Ali Khan on Wednesday war­ned that any step taken in haste and without consensus could harm the federation. “Good governance is needed in every province. But the creation of new provinces is not the only solution to improve governance, there are other ways, too. It should not be done in haste, and without consensus. It’s very good to have a discussion on this issue,” he said, while speaking to the media at the Peshawar High Court. “However, making hasty decisions, going against the will of the people, imposing own decisions [on them], bulldozing such decisions through parliament or new constitutional amendments in such times of turmoil will only add to the problems people are facing instead of resolving issues. Therefore, this should be avoided,” he said. Commenting on PTI’s planned march on Islamabad on Sept 27 , Barrister Gohar said it would be peaceful and solely a “justice march”. Expects JUI-F to join Sept 27 march; says no state resources will be used for PTI protest “The PTI’s march on Islamabad will not be a casual march. There will be no chaos, and state resources will not be used,” he said. He said PTI workers would demonstrate during the march that they were peaceful people. He added that the party had invited other opposition parties to join the protest. “We expect Maulana Fazlur Rehman and the entire joint opposition to join us in the September 27 march,” he said. Barrister Gohar said people wanted change through democratic means, with the rights of all citizens protected, and called for fresh elections. “Like the Treaty of Hudaibiyah, there should be a treaty named ‘Peace of Pakistan’, in which everyone’s rights are protected, all stakeholders are included, people are given relief and political stability is ensured,” he said. He said such a Pakistan would certainly progress and its people would prosper, adding that the public was now tired of political tension and division. He also condemned a recent statement by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, where she reportedly said Punjab faced a greater threat from neighbouring provinces than from neighbouring India. “Our core committee and political committee, in a recent meeting, demanded that the Punjab chief minister withdraw her remarks,” he said. Barrister Gohar said Pakistan’s narrative was that India and its intelligence agency, RAW, were behind terrorism in the country. “We only say that she should not support Pakistan’s enemies through her statements,” he said. Commenting on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi’s recent visit to different cities in Sindh , the PTI chairman said the chief minister had received a warm public welcome during his street campaign. “The enthusiasm among the people of Sindh regarding the upcoming protest march has boosted our morale,” he said, adding that it showed people wanted to get rid of the status quo. He said the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government was following the principles of PTI founder and former prime minister Imran Khan “in letter and spirit”. Asked about alleged police violence against students of a nursing college in Hayatabad , the PTI chairman said he was deeply saddened by the incident. He said the senior vice president of the Nursing Association had contacted him following the incident, after which he immediately approached provincial ministers Meena Khan and Khaliqur Rehman for action. Meanwhile, the PTI has submitted a list of six party leaders to the Adiala jail administration to allow them to meet incarcerated party founder Imran Khan on Thursday (today). The list, submitted by Advocate Awais Younas Chaudhry, includes Sajjad Hussain Shah, Qaiser Abbas Maan, Saqib Meraaj, Malik Shakeel, Zeeshan Mohsin and Daniyal Kiyani.
