But while their attacks on security forces have declined, these groups have not been decimated. 10 On 14 December 2025, a shooting at Sydney’s Bondi Beach claimed the lives of fifteen people at the hands of father and son, Sajid and Naveed Akram. In the weeks leading up to the attack, the duo had spent several weeks in Davao City in eastern Mindanao. While some investigative journalists suggested the journey was an attempt to establish ties with local jihadist networks, their precise motives for the trip remain unconfirmed. Crisis Group phone interviews, December 2025. Some locals fear that former militants could re-emerge. 11 Crisis Group interview, member of a peacebuilding non-governmental organisation from Maguindanao del Sur, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Remnants of the nationwide communist insurgency, the New People’s Army, also operate in parts of the region, particularly Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte. 12 Crisis Group Report N°338, Calming the Long War in the Philippine Countryside , 19 April 2024. According to government statistics, the insurgency numbers less than 1,000 fighters and no longer has any large units combining political cadres and fighters. Manila has looked to the military to patrol areas where these waning insurgencies persist. Meanwhile, the police take the lead in handling law and order in calmer areas, where guerrilla presence is negligible. Another obstacle to durable peace revolves around violent disputes over land and politics that have long plagued the region. Some of those are clan feuds, known as rido , and others are communal conflicts. These types of conflict are collectively referred to as “horizontal violence” by journalists and academics. 13 Crisis Group interview, civil society activist, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Clan feuds are comparable to vendettas. The number of shootings, particularly in Central Mindanao (Cotabato City, Maguindanao del Sur and parts of Lanao del Sur), is such that one parliamentarian described the atmosphere as “pervasive lawlessness”. 14 Crisis Group interview, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 17 February 2026. A local conflict watchdog, using data from community networks, has recorded hundreds of incidents since January 2026 alone. See “Safeguard the Bangsamoro Vote: A critical period to transcend violence in the region”, Climate Conflict Action Asia, 30 July 2026. With many local disputes escalating into large-scale clashes, the failures of both the military and police to deter shootings have become conspicuous. The upcoming parliamentary elections are likely to aggravate tensions, as rival political blocs and local elites may enlist armed groups to intimidate voters or disturb the ballot. 15 Crisis Group interview, Bangsamoro political strategist, 28 April 2026, Manila. The three local elections held in the region since its creation – in 2022, 2024 and 2025 – were less volatile than in the past but still featured high levels of violence. Infighting within the MILF is also a source of tension. 16 Crisis Group interviews, community leaders and officials, Cotabato City, 5-6 August 2026. While certain disputes stem from local resource control, deepening rifts within the MILF drive other conflicts. Frequently, these dynamics intertwine as factionalism amplifies existing land conflicts. Crisis Group interview, conflict researcher, Manila, 13 August 2026. Violence escalates quickly and frequently recurs in the region’s most conflict-affected areas, with outbreaks occurring most recently in the Special Geographic Area and parts of Maguindanao del Sur. 17 An ambush on Bangsamoro’s Chief Minister Macacua in the village of Bitu in Maguindanao del Norte by unidentified gunmen further highlighted the region’s volatility. The attack did not hurt anyone in Macacua’s convoy. Edwin Fernandez, “BARMM chief survives ambush in Maguindanao”, Inquirer , 16 August 2026. Criminal activity in the Bangsamoro also thrives wherever state authority is weak. While petty crimes such as theft or robberies are relatively rare in the region, illicit economies are ubiquitous, and have evolved in parallel to the peace process. 18 Crisis Group interviews, observers and police officers, February-March 2026. Kidnappings for ransom, which used to be Mindanao’s most lucrative business, have almost disappeared; smuggling, however, has proliferated, including for goods ranging from weapons to cooking oil. 19 Maritime Bangsamoro in particular, especially the provinces of Tawi-Tawi and Basilan, along with its former province Sulu, has traditionally been Mindanao’s “backdoor”, where many local communities have long treated smuggling to and from the Malaysian state of Sabah as legitimate commerce. In Central Mindanao, illicit cigarette trading has also flourished, much of it supplied from Indonesia and Vietnam and allegedly shielded by local powerbrokers. Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026; diplomats, Manila, 30 April 2026. See also, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, “ An Interconnected Criminal Ecosystem: Transnational Organized Crime Threat Assessment for South-East Asia ”, July 2026, pp. 216-217. This illicit activity, however, has not led to open violence between competing criminal interests as syndicates appear to work with local governments rather than against them, and turf wars are scarce. Human trafficking across the region, especially involving women, also remains a concern given the region’s porous borders and long coastlines. 20 See for example, Lean Bolongon, “Safeguarding minors: Combating illegal recruitment in BARMM”, Philippine Information Agency , 17 March 2026. Another profitable business in Mindanao is the drug trade. During former President Rodrigo Duterte’s term in office from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine police carried out a nation-wide anti-drug campaign that targeted suspected dealers and users, killing thousands. 21 Georgi Engelbrecht, “Philippines: The International Criminal Court Goes After Duterte’s Drug War”, 17 September 2021. While some Mindanao drug lords were killed, other networks survived and have since flourished. 22 Crisis Group interview, security analyst, Manila, 10 March 2026. As early as 2023 – just a year after Duterte left office – a local activist in Marawi declared that the “drugs are back”. 23 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 26 October 2023. The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency and the police continue counter-narcotic operations; some locals say they have recently seen an increase in arrests and shoot-outs. 24 Crisis Group has recorded at least ten such anti-drug operations across the region in 2026 so far. One clash in August between security forces and an armed drug trafficking outfit in Bongao town in Tawi-Tawi left one person dead and three others wounded, including a naval officer. 25 Edwin Fernandez, “PDEA agent, drug suspect killed; 3 Marines wounded in Tawi-Tawi”, Inquirer , 9 August 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power. The proliferation of firearms has also contributed to conflict and crime in the region. 26 It is notoriously hard to determine the total number of guns in the region. In late 2024, the police estimated that the region had over 27,000 unregistered firearms, while a well-informed interlocutor told Crisis Group that there were 20,000 legally registered ones. Crisis Group interview, 11 February 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power; decades of war have made weapons ubiquitous. 27 Individuals and clans carry a wide variety of weapons, ranging from antiquated rifles to machine guns. Other Philippine regions where guns are prevalent are Abra and Negros. Members of armed groups and many local politicians, civilians and ex-combatants carry these weapons. 28 The first armed movement in the region, the MNLF, despite having splintered into factions, also retains weapons. The 1996 peace agreement with the movement sidestepped the question of disarmament, but in the absence of any attacks on government forces by a MNLF faction since 2012, Manila tolerates the awkward status quo of hundreds of MNLF fighters still being under arms. Crisis Group interviews, MNLF political cadre, Cotabato City, 16 February 2026. Under the 2014 peace agreement, the MILF has taken part in the gradual demobilisation of its forces. In early 2026, however, the group stopped formally participating in the process and other normalisation activities such high-level meetings due to Manila’s perceived failure to fulfil promises of socio-economic benefits for combatants who lay down their arms; 14,000 fighters have still to be decommissioned, along with 2,450 weapons. 29 Taher Solaiman, “MILF declares ‘temporary pause’ in peace process engagement with national government”, Luwaran.com , 17 March 2026. Following discussions between its peace panel and government counterparts, the MILF ended the temporary suspension of its engagement in the peace process in early August, but demobilisation of rebels appears to still be on hold. 30 Carolyn Arguillas, “GPH-MILF Peace Implementing Panels finally meet; MILF’s ‘temporary pause’ lifted”, Mindanews , 5 August 2026. While there has been a proliferation of Philippine gun laws over the past five decades, they are strikingly permissive. Under a so-called Type 5 licence, for example, Filipinos are allowed to possess up to fifteen firearms. Existing ordinances, moreover, are loosely enforced. Individuals often acquire weapons legally but then remove their serial numbers, making them untraceable. 31 Crisis Group interview, police officer, Manila, 10 May 2026. Consequently, the government’s main focus is on the pool of “loose” firearms – those guns which the state cannot trace or document – with the goal of either seizing them or persuading politicians and civilians to turn them in. 32 The term “loose firearms” refers broadly to weapons that rebels, criminals or civilians hold without proper registration, including those purchased legally but later left unregistered or with expired licenses. But the task is overwhelming; civil society activists say guns continue to flow in and out of the Bangsamoro without any means to trace them. 33 Crisis Group phone interview, source from Basilan, 28 February 2026. High-calibre weapons such as mortars, machine guns or assault rifles can easily stoke local conflicts as their lethality increases the likelihood of casualties and tit-for-tat retaliation. 34 On 2 August, national police chief Jose Nartatez pushed for a crackdown on illegal firearms and armed groups in the region ahead of the September polls. Andrea Gregorio, “PNP ramps up ops vs gun-for-hire groups ahead of BARMM polls”, Inquirer , 2 August 2026. For its part, the interim regional government has only recently started discussing a bill to regulate firearms and ammunition in the autonomous region. 35 Member of parliament Omar Sema filed the bill on 16 April 2026, marking the sole instance that such legislation has been discussed in the regional parliament, out of the 469 bills it has passed so far. In the meantime, local governments such as the province of Basilan have launched programs to collect small arms and light weapons. This effort is being done in coordination with the national peace process office and is underwritten by foreign donors. Buy-in, however, has been uneven. 36 An obstacle to these schemes is that the market value of firearms often surpasses the cash incentives offered to rebels or civilians for surrendering them. Two senior military commanders expressed deep scepticism about the campaign, arguing that the initiative would have no meaningful impact on the security landscape, was far too modest in scale, and targeted the wrong weapons (those not in the hands of rebels or ex-combatants). Crisis Group interviews, Maguindanao and Cotabato, February-March 2026. Other proposed solutions, such as forced mass disarmament or the comprehensive registration of firearms, do not seem realistic in the Bangsamoro context. 37 Crisis Group interviews, interim government officials and civil society representatives, Cotabato City, February-March 2026. Efforts to create “zones of peace” or “gun-free zones”, often initiated by non-government organisations, have been short-lived. 38 Crisis Group interview, head of a civil society organisation, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. A checkpoint during the 2024 village polls in Lanao del Sur, Philippines. February 2024. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht B. Policing under Autonomy To meet the challenge of the post-conflict landscape, the drafters of the 2014 peace agreement had to think hard about the best way to police the region. 39 During the peace talks, policing was a key subject – as contentious as it was during negotiations between the government and the MNLF in 1996. That peace agreement contained no provisions for disarmament or demobilisation, and clashes continued to flare more than a decade after the deal. While the 1996 agreement envisaged integrating MNLF rebels into state forces, only a quarter of the insurgent force eventually joined the police or military, voluntarily bringing with them more than 4,000 firearms Crisis Group interview, military officer, Manila, 26 February 2026. See also, Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, “Integration of MNLF forces into the PNP and AFP: Integration without demobilization and disarmament”, unpublished paper for UP Center on Integrative and Development Studies project on the GRP-MNLF peace agreement, 2000. The agreement called for a regional police force that was to be “civilian in character, effective and efficient in law enforcement, fair and impartial, and accountable under the law for its actions”, and whose mandate would be “law enforcement and maintenance of peace and order” in the region. 40 Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro and Annex on Normalisation . But the division of labour between Manila, its national police force and the region remained ambiguous. 41 The Philippine National Police, created in 1991, is tasked with preventing and investigating criminal activities and strengthening internal security. The Department of Interior and Local Government has political control over the force, while the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) administers and disciplines it. The president selects the national police chief and senior police officers and appoints the secretary of the department of interior and local government. Headquartered in Manila, the force maintains regional, provincial and municipal stations across the archipelago, but also includes two specialised units: the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group focuses on organised crime and terrorism; the Special Action Force, the PNP’s elite commando unit, is in charge of counterterrorism, hostage rescue, and high-risk operations as well as ad hoc tasks such as patrolling hot spots during elections. One part of the agreement stipulated that the regional government, working in coordination with Manila, “shall have primary responsibility over public order and safety within the Bangsamoro”. 42 Annex on Power Sharing , Art. II, 14. In another part, the accord said the police force is “responsible both to the central government and the Bangsamoro government”. 43 Framework Agreement and Annex on Normalisation. The Philippine Constitution is clear in that regard, as Art. 10 Section 21 states: “The preservation of peace and order within the regions shall be the responsibility of the local police agencies which shall be organised, maintained, supervised, and utilised in accordance with applicable laws. The defence and security of the regions shall be the responsibility of the National Government”. Government officials involved in the negotiations say the agreement was clear the regional police would remain under national authority. 44 One official involved in the process, however, said that Manila dodged the hard questions until the end, keeping the wording intentionally vague, and ended up “parking” the issue for the future. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 31 July 2026. The MILF, however, maintains that the common understanding in talks was that policing should be under the control of the autonomous government. The agreement also set up an Independent Commission on Policing to determine how law enforcement should function in the new region. When the commission delivered its report in April 2014, it recommended that the force remain a part of the national police, but stressed that it should invest in community‑based policing. 45 The Independent Commission on Policing for the Bangsamoro, “Policing for the Bangsamoro”, 2014. Report on file with Crisis Group. Community policing is generally understood as an approach that builds active partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to solve community problems and jointly ensure public safety. The commission highlighted the need for community policing that respects human rights and Sharia law. Another problem the commission identified was the police’s weak accountability to the communities they serve. Tasked with translating the occasionally vague peace agreement into clear and legally binding terms, the 2019 autonomy law dismissed the idea of a separate Bangsamoro police force. Wary of clashing with the 1987 constitution’s centralised approach to policing, lawmakers assigned public order and safety to the national government. 46 A single national police force was mandated to curb the historical misuse of local law enforcement by warlords. Yet mindful of the authoritarian practices during Martial Law under Ferdinand Marcos, the constitution balanced this by granting local governments a supervisory role to ensure checks and balances. This outcome reflected the stance of former President Rodrigo Duterte, who was in office when the autonomy law came into force, but both the national police force and lawyers were also sceptical about proposals for a separate regional police force. 47 Crisis Group telephone interview, analyst, 18 February 2021. In early 2019, the national police established a Police Regional Office (PRO-BARMM), which is part of the national police and therefore firmly under Manila’s control. 48 According to most observers and local figures, any change to this status quo needs constitutional amendments. Crisis Group written communication, 12 June 2026. See also, Nash Maulana, “‘BARMM police, Moro Senate seat require Charter change”, Manila Standard , 3 May 2026. At the same time, the organic law included two compromise provisions. The first one was to allow the integration of MILF and MNLF members into PRO-BARMM (see Section III.A.2). 49 The MILF was critical towards integration of their forces into the police during the peace talks. Later, however, the movement accepted this provision in the autonomy law. The second one called for the chief of the regional police force to be appointed “upon consultation with the Chief Minister”. In practice, however, it is the national police chief who has ultimately decided on this appointment. 50 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 27 February 2026. In late 2025, however, a national police commission resolution reiterated that the region’s chief minister can both recommend candidates and provide feedback on shortlisted officers. III. Security and Justice in Transition Various bodies in the Bangsamoro region are responsible for tackling flare-ups of violence. While the police and military remain central to maintaining order, other government and community institutions also help dispense justice and mediate disputes. A. The Police during the Bangsamoro Transition As is the case with the national police as a whole, the Bangsamoro force is hierarchical in nature. Its regional headquarters are in Parang, from which it oversees five provincial headquarters and more than one hundred municipal police stations. Every town has a team of officers who mostly take care of basic law enforcement. These tasks include investigating crimes, preparing requests for warrants or subpoenas from the courts, dealing with minor offences and arresting criminals and insurgents. 51 Arrest powers remain outside the military’s purview, except in instances of “in flagrante delicto” where troops directly witness a crime. The number of officers in the region is, by many accounts, insufficient: a regular station typically has a staff of a bit over twenty, covering municipalities with populations as large as 25,000. Overall, the police force’s headcount stands at over 7,000. 52 Crisis Group interviews, police officers, Cotabato City and Parang, 6-7 August 2026. Every municipal police chief shapes the local force’s policies on everything from community engagement and collaboration with politicians to defining how to handle local conflicts. In the post-2019 transition period, the police has emphasised anti-drug operations and curbing the spread of illegal firearms. 53 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. These priorities stem from the national government’s priority of combating drugs, as well as community support for the campaign. 54 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Cotabato City, 6 August 2026. Given their limited numbers and lack of equipment, it has been more difficult for the police to address complex clan feuds, which can flare up without forewarning. In the most conflict-affected parts of Maguindanao, the police struggle to conduct even routine patrols, leaving law and order in the military’s hands. 55 A police chief from the region distinguished between “law enforcement”, for which the police is in the lead, and “combat operations” that are the domain of the military. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 17 February 2026. A senior police officer said the force can take care of so-called “soft targets”, but still need back-up if the operation occurs in a “harsh” context. 56 Crisis Group interview, Shariff Aguak, Maguindanao del Sur, 27 March 2026. According to one regional bureaucrat, the police may be willing to take over internal security but is currently “not capable” of doing so. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Perceptions of law enforcers vary. The police appear more connected to everyday life than the military because their stations are located near town halls, making them visibly present. Some officers have a genuine desire to help their communities. But for many young Moro men and women, becoming a police officer is more about acquiring a secure job than answering the call of duty. 57 Crisis Group interview, member of parliament, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 13 February 2026; academic, Marawi City, 27 March 2026. Some locals are also sceptical about the ability of the police to respond to incidents. 58 In Lanao del Sur, a civil society activist also observed the police are too slow to respond to violence. Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. Locals in predominantly non-Moro Indigenous communities also feel that law enforcement does not always respond to their concerns. 59 Crisis Group interview, phone interview, community leader, 6 December 2021; online communication, peace process observer, 17 August 2026. That said, several surveys show the police enjoy a degree of trust from local people. 60 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 20 March 2026. Surveys made available to Crisis Group. Other survey data suggests that many residents continue to look to local leaders and religious figures for security. Tatsuya Koyama, “Who Supports the Peace? A Survey of Postconflict Public Opinion in Maguindanao, the Philippines”, Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs , vol. 44 no. 3 (December 2025). At the beginning of the transition, many MILF commanders hoped community policing – namely, building partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to ensure public safety – would become widespread. 61 Crisis Group interview, senior MILF commander, Cotabato City, 27 November 2019. The Philippine police have used civilian auxiliaries known as the Barangay Peace Action Teams (BPATs) and Civilian Volunteer Organisations (CVOs) that came closest to community policing. With police approval, BPATs may carry light firearms. CVOs focus on intelligence gathering, neighbourhood patrols, and emergency response. Officially unarmed, they may use weapons when supporting police operations, although in practice some mayors or village heads have been known to issue them firearms. Despite the support of international donors, however, and its inclusion in the Philippine policing doctrine, this approach never really gained momentum. 62 Crisis Group interview, donor official, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Police officers admit that resource limitations, understaffing and local politics complicate the work of fostering stronger relations with Bangsamoro communities. 63 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato and Parang, 5-7 August 2026. Even so, some individual officers have been more proactive. A former police chief in Maguindanao, for example, instructed his officers to visit communities and engage residents on important concerns, at times accompanied by representatives from the judicial system. 64 This community outreach mostly relates to drugs and firearms use. Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. As for efforts to integrate MILF fighters into the police force, as stipulated in the autonomy law (see Section II.B), these have so far had limited success. In 2019, the government waived height, age, and education requirements for five years to allow more former MILF (and MNLF) rebels to qualify for recruitment in the regional force. After a two-year interruption due to the COVID-19 pandemic, 11,075 applicants took a special eligibility exam in May 2022, which 7,145 passed. Yet in the years that followed, the government earmarked only about 400 positions for the former fighters, and just 396 joined the police force. 65 At present, 36 women were considered for recruitment and have undergone on-the-job-training in police stations across the region. “The Peace Accords Matrix – Mindanao (PAM-M) and Civil Society Normalization Update Report (January-April 2026)”, University of Notre Dame, 3 August 2026, p. 11. While the interim government stepped in to fund their training, Manila subsequently grew sceptical of maintaining dedicated quotas for ex-rebels, and future applicants will have to compete within the general pool of all Filipinos vying for the 1,500 police positions available annually. 66 Third Party Monitoring Team, 9th public report, 5 May 2026, p. 61. A small concession was a resolution by the national police commission in July 2025, which extended the police application deadline for MILF and MNLF members to 8 June 2027. Bong Sarmiento, “MILF, MNLF members who want to become cops can apply until June 2027”, Inquirer , 17 July 2025. While they may not have joined in large numbers, the former MILF fighters now working as police officers appear to have integrated smoothly. While they may not have joined in large numbers, the former MILF fighters now working as police officers appear to have integrated smoothly. 67 Crisis Group interview, Manila, international observer, 21 October 2022. Police officers from Cotabato City said MILF recruits have been well‑received by their new colleagues, and a sense of camaraderie now animates the ranks. 68 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 28 March 2026, 6 August 2026. The Third Party Monitoring Team – an independent body mandated with overseeing the peace process – has encouraged further recruitment, underlining it “could serve as a powerful symbol of previously warring entities working constructively to build a secure future together”. 69 Third Party Monitoring Team, 9th public report, 5 May 2026, p. 61. But prospects for further integration appear dim. Manila has demonstrated no appetite to reintroduce a quota for ex-rebels or hire Moro who passed the exam but were not incorporated into the force. A part of the MILF, furthermore, still expects the regional government to take over policing in the region in the long term. 70 Crisis Group interview, international observer, Manila, 14 October 2022. Crisis Group interviews, MILF officials, February-March 2026. In this sense, the policing issue is emblematic of a broader lack of agreement on the future of the peace process. 71 Crisis Group interviews, international and local observers, Cotabato and Manila, February-March 2026. Marking its new secretary’s first 100 days, the Philippine peace process office’s late-July report made no mention of policing. Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity, July 2026. A mural near the regional police headquarters in Parang, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht B. The Role of the Armed Forces While the region is immersed in a transition marked by ongoing episodes of violence, the superior operational capacity of the Armed Forces of the Philippines means that they remain in charge of most aspects of Bangsamoro security. In terms of force structure, the military has three infantry divisions across the region and two other divisions backing its northern and south-eastern flanks. 72 The 6th Infantry Division is in Awang, Maguindanao del Norte; the 1st Infantry Division in Pagadian, Zamboanga del Sur; the 11th Infantry Division in Jolo, Sulu; the 4th Infantry Division in Cagayan de Oro and the 10th Infantry Division in Davao City. Light infantry battalions are based in population centres, with companies deployed in key towns or villages. 73 A senior officer argued the military is the most visible manifestation of the state in some villages and enjoys more legitimacy than police, courts or local politicians due to better logistics, disaster response capabilities and ability to withstand clan capture. Crisis Group online communication, navy officer, 16 June 2026. Part of the military’s acceptability is also its commitment to the ceasefire with the MILF. To boost its reach, the military has also employed so-called force multipliers. These include paramilitary forces such as the Citizen Armed Force Geographical Units (CAFGUs). 74 President Corazon Aquino established CAFGUs in 1987 to help meet the challenges posed by communist and Moro insurgents. Aquino’s successor, Fidel Ramos, sought to scale back auxiliaries during the 1990s, but in 2001 President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, confronted with mounting internal threats, expanded their ranks once more. Since then, CAFGU contingents have steadily grown. The CAFGU Active Auxiliaries serve fifteen days a month and are integrated into the army’s chain of command; the Special CAFGU Active Auxiliaries operations also fall under the formal authority of the armed forces but local governments or private firms pay for them to guard businesses or secure territory. From the perspective of the military’s central command, maintaining these auxiliaries – which have tens of thousands of members – is more cost‑effective than expanding the regular force. 75 At least one government official told Crisis Group there is a cap now on CAFGU recruitment in Mindanao. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 27 February 2026. In some conversations with Crisis Group, however, commanders still pushed for CAFGU recruitment. Observers also noted recent training in areas such as Lanao. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 15 March 2026. Critics, however, express concern about lack of discipline, and say these paramilitaries are at risk of becoming private militias answerable to kinship networks or to whichever group pays them. They also get involved in local land disputes, either as direct party to the conflict or at the behest of landowners. 76 Crisis Group interviews, civil society activist, Marawi, 26 October 2023; MILF member, Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, 28 March 2026. The military’s priorities in the region have shifted over the last seven years. The military’s priorities in the region have shifted over the last seven years. At the beginning of the transition, especially in areas where insurgent and militant activity was concentrated, the military focused on high-value targets and combat operations, leaving the maintenance of “local peace” to the police. 77 Crisis Group telephone interview, security analyst in Sulu, 24 August 2021. As the threat level associated with militant groups decreased, relations between local residents and military personnel have improved. 78 In the past, communities were fearful of the armed forces, but the Bangsamoro peace process has altered that perception, even if many locals do not forget the military’s past abuses and heavy‑handed operations in their areas. A key task for the army has since become that of “managing” the MILF: while waiting for the decommissioning of the ex-rebels, troops need to control the fall-out of internal feuds emanating from the movement’s involvement in local politics. 79 Officers try to keep community disputes in check by supporting conflict resolution, though there are variations in how they go about this. Crisis Group interviews, military officers, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 16 February 2026. Concern about rebel resurgence shapes military commanders’ threat perceptions, but from the division level down to the battalion, officers maintain fluid communication channels with their MILF counterparts. 80 Crisis Group interviews, military commanders, Lanao and Maguindanao, January-April 2026. The peace agreement foresaw the military redeploying outside the Bangsamoro, a move that military leadership should now be keener to make given the country’s shift of focus toward external defence. 81 See Crisis Group Asia Report N°349, Riding Unruly Waves: The Philippines’ Military Modernisation Effort , 12 August 2025. But beyond existing “rotational rationalisation”, which happens on a regular basis, military leaders have been cautious about reducing their footprint in the region. 82 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 26 February 2026. Redeploying the military was part of the peace agreement but has made only limited progress. For one thing, residual violence persists in Mindanao. 83 Crisis Group interview, foreign military adviser, Manila, 29 May 2026. There are fears that a sizeable withdrawal would leave a vacuum, with neither reserve forces nor police ready to step in. 84 A military assessment said that “apart from the intensified checkpoint operations, the police must proactively target criminals and private armed groups that may influence the election process”. Report made available to Crisis Group. A regional bureaucrat admitted that given the reach and intensity of local conflict, it would be good “to keep the military where it is”. 85 Crisis Group interview, bureaucrat, Cotabato City, 15 February 2026. There is a legal reason for the hesitation as well. Philippine law assigns the military primary authority over combating internal threats; for the police to assume control, these laws would have to be amended. 86 Crisis Group interviews, security officials, Manila, 4 February 2026. Examples include Republic Act No. 8551 of 1998, which restored the military’s primary role in suppressing insurgency and internal threats while assigning a supporting function to the police, and the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020, which gives surveillance and intelligence-gathering authority to both police and the armed forces. Members of the military – especially those in the army – also benefit from the current setup. Divisions and brigades wield not only military authority but also economic clout as they generate local jobs and may receive funds from local authorities. 87 Crisis Group interview, military officer, Manila, 22 June 2024. In addition, the armed forces’ current metrics for performance evaluation and promotion do not encourage a shift in priorities, with experience in counter-insurgency efforts still helping to boost officers’ career prospects. C. Law, Justice and Conflict Resolution The peace agreement and the autonomy law recognised that in order for the Bangsamoro to exercise self-governance, it will need a system of justice that reflects the region’s culture and values. The region’s citizens have various legal regimes to choose from. 88 Art. X of the Bangsamoro Organic Law . The regular Philippine judicial system functions through municipal and regional trial courts, ensuring access to common legal processes. These extend down to the community level, where the barangay or village justice system also provides a formal venue for resolving local disputes. 89 The barangay is the smallest unit of political administration in the Philippines, generally accounting for a cluster of villages. The village justice system, mandated by Philippine law since 1991, comprises local councils that are tasked with mediating disputes before they reach formal courts. Settling a dispute at the village level, however, does not guarantee it will not reignite. Crisis Group interview, Bangsamoro lawyer, Cotabato City, 5 August 2026. Moro and other Indigenous communities maintain their own justice practices. Rooted in custom rather than formal litigation, these systems remain outside direct government oversight yet enjoy the support of local people. Relying on individuals with no or minimal formal association with the state, these processes typically lead to amicable settlements. 90 Crisis Group phone interview, 17 August 2021. See also, Raihan A. Yusoph, “Hybridizing Justice: Cultural Legitimacy and the Limits of Traditional Dispute Resolution in Lanao del Sur, the Philippines”, Asian Journal of Peacebuilding , vol. 13 no. 2 (November 2025), pp. 207-230. Sharia, or Islamic law, also applies to Muslims in the region if they choose to submit to it. Under the supervision of the Philippine Supreme Court, several Sharia courts handle family matters and personal affairs, such as divorce or inheritance. 91 Ferdinand Marcos Sr. created Sharia courts in the Philippines in 1977 as a measure to curb the influence of the Moro rebellion in Mindanao. The peace agreement strengthened this type of jurisdiction. 92 While the MILF had originally envisioned a broader application of Sharia law, the autonomy law ensured the region’s jurisdiction did not extend beyond the Philippine constitution’s limits. Crisis Group interview, MILF official, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. Some local MILF authorities, such as community camps or commanders, also maintain their own Sharia jurisdictions. 93 The MILF officially pronounced its Sharia courts dissolved a few years ago, but the informal system still functions in some areas. Sometimes, communities perceive the Sharia courts’ actions as overreach. Crisis Group interview, local civil society activist, Cotabato City, 15 February 2026. But views differ across the Bangsamoro as to the desired scope of Islamic law. Many MILF cadres would welcome Sharia as the main legal system. 94 Crisis Group interview, senior MILF commander, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 26 October 2022. Some non-MILF members also think Sharia could “decongest” cases for Muslims in public courts, and strengthen the rule of law among Moro communities. 95 Crisis Group interview, 11 February, source from Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Other Moro Muslims, however, prefer the public court system, given that it is still the most official route and enforcement is at least formally guaranteed, over traditional mechanisms, which are perceived to be quick but less authoritative. 96 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 27 March 2026. Bangsamoro citizens use these different justice mechanisms – whether traditional mediation, Sharia or public courts – depending on the types of issues at hand, but also based on their class, gender or ethno-linguistic group. While in principle this “forum shopping” arrangement can be useful, problems arise if conflict parties such as former rebels, clans or insurgents fail to accept resolutions from these various judicial bodies, leading to disputes resurfacing and becoming more violent. [The] legal fragmentation makes Bangsamoro institutions offering routes to conflict resolution all the more important. This legal fragmentation makes Bangsamoro institutions offering routes to conflict resolution all the more important. The interim government has several bodies dealing with public safety, the most important of which is the Ministry for Public Order and Safety, whose mandate is to prevent and resolve clan feuds that have long destabilised the region. That said, the ministry’s small budget has left it with limited reach. 97 The Ministry for Public Order and Safety and some legislators have often channelled large sums to feuding clans as an inducement to settle. The ministry has also provided training to local community monitors. Initial hurdles at the outset of the transition, however, especially regarding the ministry’s precise mandate, and internal friction within the bureaucracy, have all hampered its effectiveness. Crisis Group interview, local analyst, 18 August 2026. In addition, as local conflict was rising around 2022, the chief minister created the Peace, Security and Reconciliation Office, whose mandate overlaps with the ministry but focuses more narrowly on disputes among MILF members. Leadership changes, however, have reduced the office’s effectiveness. 98 Crisis Group phone interview, analyst, 5 June 2026. Critics argue that the office’s impact has waned under the current director, Castro Emran, citing a perceived loyalty to the region’s chief minister over the MILF chairman, whose rival factions now compete with one another for political influence and mass support. More generally, many observers view him as less proactive in resolving issues than his predecessor, Anwar Alamada. Local government officials, meanwhile, constitute the first line of political authority, and are also crucial in dealing with outbreaks of conflict. They do this in two main ways. First, local mayors or village captains have the mandate to fix local disputes in their town or village. Secondly, they chair peace and order councils, which bring together officials, security personnel (including police chiefs and senior military commanders) and community representatives to coordinate responses when violence erupts. 99 Crisis Group interview, expert, M’lang, Cotabato province, 29 October 2023. Some councils meet regularly, thereby also playing a conflict prevention role, but others convene only after unrest has broken out. In many cases, the convening of the councils is a formality but does not make a dent on disputes. 100 Crisis Group interview, senior national security official, Manila, 25 March 2026. “They are often just talk shops”, quipped a military officer. 101 Crisis Group interview, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 28 March 2026. Finally, the peace agreement created Joint Peace and Security Teams – hybrid units comprising police, military and MILF personnel. While these are now deployed across 24 locations, they have limited mobility and only a few teams actually seek to manage conflicts. 102 Summary Report made available to Crisis Group, BARMM Peace Conference 2025, “From Consultation to Action – Advancing Peace Together”, p. 8. For instance, despite the presence of a team in parts of former Pikit town – a notorious conflict hotspot until a few years ago – a local noted that its effect on deterring violence or settling disputes is minimal. 103 Crisis Group interview, security manager of a non-governmental organisation, Cotabato City, 10 February 2026; local observer, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Some observers view their creation as purely symbolic – a confidence-building measure between Manila and the MILF, which is valued for their mere presence more than their real contribution. 104 Crisis Group interviews, local security analysts, Cotabato City, 9-10 February 2026. A local court building in Cotabato City, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht IV. Overcoming Community Insecurity Despite – or because of – a complex web of overlapping peacebuilding institutions, the Bangsamoro region is struggling to deliver the payoff autonomy was supposed to bring. Multiple actors – including the police, regional ministries, and municipal governments – help keep the peace. This system reflects a desire to prevent any one entity from becoming too dominant. But in practice this diffusion of authority means the underlying sources of conflict often go unaddressed. A. Law Enforcement Challenges Policing in the region is complicated by a thicket of operational challenges. As stated previously, communities in the BARMM require more police than current resources allow. The region’s geography, which includes porous coastlines, rugged and mountainous terrain, as well as isolated villages, further slows operations and inhibits deployment. With units overstretched, municipal forces struggle to deter clan feuds and must often wait for military reinforcements. In addition, equipment and training gaps persist, from forensic capacity to the absence of high power firearms or even patrol cars. 105 Crisis Group interview, policing expert, Manila, 12 May 2026. Locals also allege that, despite their mandate to safeguard lives and property, police officers tend to neglect investigating crimes unless citizens formally report them. 106 Crisis Group interviews, local community observers, Lanao and Maguindanao, February-March 2026. Finally, when feuds erupt in communities, police officers sometimes hesitate to respond because they fear they and their families could be dragged into the dispute. 107 Crisis Group interviews, military commander and community members, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. Allegations of corruption further undermine the police’s effectiveness. Theft or illicit sales of police weapons and ammunition has meant that on occasion arms meant for law enforcement have ended up in the hands of those it seeks to fight. 108 In 2018, for example, more than a thousand Kalashnikov AK‑47 rifles that the Philippine National Police issued found their way to communist insurgents, leading to graft and falsification charges against senior police officers. See also, Barbara Dacanay, “Manila: Top ranking policemen accused of selling high-powered firearms”, Gulf News , 15 September 2018. Anecdotal evidence indicates that some police force candidates effectively purchase their positions, and may look for more economic payoffs once in their posts. Observers also noted that the drug war under former President Duterte left its mark on the police, both in shaping the institution – heavy-handedness has become the norm – and through the practice of reassigning underperforming officers to Mindanao. 109 Crisis Group interview, security expert, Manila, 2 February 2026. Police officers that are well-trained and have a solid grasp of the region, on the other hand, are not always tapped for their expertise by commanders in the national force. 110 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 30 March 2026. Aligning law enforcement institutions with the peace process and ceasefires has proven far more challenging than it has with the military. Aligning law enforcement institutions with the peace process and ceasefires has proven far more challenging than it has with the military, which had more exposure to armed violence. This has resulted in several clashes between police and the MILF, as law enforcement officers failed to coordinate with the ex-rebels when conducting raids. More broadly, members of institutions such as the National Police Commission, and even senior police officers assigned to the region, especially when they are new, struggle to understand certain requirements of the peace process such as ceasefire protocols, largely because national authorities fail to properly explain to them why they matter. 111 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 27 February 2026. Perhaps the biggest issue concerns the national police’s accountability. In the Philippines, political influence on the police extends across all levels, encompassing provinces, cities, and municipalities alike. This happens because local officeholders, whether mayors or provincial governors, are automatically deputised as representatives on the National Police Commission, which supervises the work of the force. Political influence comes in two ways. First, governors and mayors play a key role in selecting officers for the positions of provincial or municipal police chief. Secondly, officials also have the power to direct and oversee the day-to-day functions of police in their area. 112 Philippine law, through Republic Act 6975, grants local chief executives “operational supervision and control” over police units, defined as the authority to direct, oversee, and inspect their operations. Mayors exercise considerable financial influence by providing essential equipment and operational funds that the central government fails to supply, often making the national police dependent on local government support. In the worst case, police officers even end up taking part in local politicians’ so-called private armies. Powerful figures hold different perspectives on how – or whether – to deal with political influence on the police. Some members of the MILF and the bureaucracy clearly wish the police would have no ties with local politicians, whereas political clans and local officials, unsurprisingly, are keen to preserve the status quo. 113 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, February-March 2026. Some military commanders Crisis Group spoke to also said that the police’s links to local politicians render the force “less effective”. 114 Crisis Group interview, commanders, Central Mindanao, February 2026. B. Fragmented and Politicised Institutions Another difficulty arises from the overlapping jurisdictions of the national government, the regional administration and local governments. Although the police and military are officially in charge of security, in practice the autonomous government – not to mention provincial and municipal authorities – often step in. This can result in all parties asserting responsibility, but only to the point they find convenient. For instance, even if regional guidelines on settling clan feuds are in place, personalities in localities where conflict erupts often matter more than institutions in curbing them. 115 Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. In addition, while the regional government has some prerogatives (see Section III.C), it does not stand above the security forces’ chain of command. To borrow the words of a local clan leader, all this means that the regional administration only has a “semblance” of authority. 116 Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 26 October 2022. Mayors, on the other hand, shift between resolving local issues when it works to their advantage or passing the buck to higher authorities or the military when it does not. Another concern is the interaction between the police and the military, which sometimes compete for authority, at times giving rise to a “power play”, as an observer who has worked with both institutions put it. 117 Crisis Group interview, Crisis Group, 11 February 2026. Intelligence sharing between the armed forces and the police, for instance, has proven difficult, and the lack of clarity in the division of labour between the two forces can blur accountability to the state and citizens if operations go wrong. 118 Crisis Group interview, former senior military intelligence officer, 20 March 2026. Intelligence sharing is particularly problematic when the target of an operation has relatives within the police force. The Joint Peace and Security Coordinating Center, a mechanism established in 2010, is tasked with coordinating military, police and coast guard operations across the country. At present, however, it mostly focuses on convening meetings and information exchanges. 119 The national police chief has acknowledged that “initiatives must translate to visible action on the ground”. Christopher Lloyd Caliwan, “PNP, AFP, PCG boost operational capabilities amid evolving threats”, Philippine News Agency, 6 March 2026. Although local conflicts are on the rise, no regional institution appears ready to grapple with the fault lines within communities. 120 Crisis Group interviews, former regional official, Cotabato City, 26 March 2006; civil society activist, Cotabato City, 7 August 2026. There is little incentive for peacebuilding in the Bangsamoro while the MILF Central Committee, regional officials aligned with Chief Minister Macacua and clans (who run local governments) are distracted by the push to outmanoeuvre one another politically and campaign for elections. Some bureaucrats, for their part, are also affected by the MILF schism and hesitate to advance peace initiatives, fearing their efforts will either be ignored or exploited by higher-ranking officials. In parts of Maguindanao, for instance, settling clan feuds often serves as a vehicle for powerbrokers to cultivate influence over MILF commanders, rather than a genuine effort to resolve disputes. 121 Crisis Group interviews, sources from Maguindanao, Cotabato City, 5 and 7 August 2026. C. Shortcomings of the Justice System A flawed justice system further undermines police effectiveness since it corrodes the rule of law and creates incentives for people to take the law into their own hands. Memories of decades of conflict, regular bursts of violence and communities’ past experiences with state authority make it difficult to make the rule of law more than “an abstract concept”. 122 Crisis Group interview, civil society leader, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Furthermore, the area is not immune to violence directed at members of the judiciary, either to scare them away or exact vengeance. 123 See for example, John Unson, “Maguindanao’s deputy provincial prosecutor, 2 companions hurt in ambush”, Philippine Star , 21 February 2020. High-profile incidents have become more scarce in recent years. Public perceptions of the justice system are shaped by its slow pace. Public courts struggle with chronic understaffing and backlogs. Judges sometimes postpone hearings because they are overloaded with cases, rotate in and out of the region, or cannot travel safely to remote municipalities. For ordinary residents, going to court is a costly ordeal, requiring time and resources many do not have. Public Sharia courts, often considered alternative venues for justice, also do not have enough judges, prosecutors and lawyers, leading to delays. 124 Crisis Group interview, MILF cadre, 12 February 2026. Sharia judges need to pass both the conventional bar and Sharia examinations. Some Islamic law students in Mindanao see this as a hindrance. MILF courts also often fail to live up to expectations. 125 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 10 December 2019; legal expert, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. A big obstacle to a well-functioning judiciary in the Bangsamoro is that powerful elites profit from a compromised system. A big obstacle to a well-functioning judiciary in the Bangsamoro is that powerful elites profit from a compromised system. A police officer observed that influential local elites at times encourage the force not to file cases against criminals, and that courts often dismiss the charges if local powerbrokers are involved. 126 Crisis Group interviews, Maguindanao del Norte, 26 March 2026. A well-off member of an influential clan, for example, said that despite his closeness to a prosecutor, the court is not likely to initiate action over the murder of one of his clan’s members given the perpetrator’s family is equally, if not more, influential. 127 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 28 April 2026. The weak rule of law can also perpetuate conflict. For example in murder cases, members of smaller clans face the dilemma of whether to file a legal case, which can result in retaliation from their opponents, or retaliate themselves, which could spark a cycle of vendettas. As a result, families sometimes choose revenge over a tedious and cumbersome legal process. In other words, the “culture of impunity” associated with the decades of conflict still exists. 128 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. A military officer with a long history in the region acknowledged that the justice system is “dysfunctional”. 129 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. D. A Stopgap Peace A major challenge to peace in the Bangsamoro is the fact that security forces remain unable to stem the horizontal violence that plagues the region. The problem persists in part because they tend to manage localised conflicts rather than resolve them, leaving space for violence to resurface. When clashes erupt, in some cases violence continues for hours before the military, which is typically the first responder, steps in. Beyond the physical dangers that communities face, these experiences undermine public perceptions of the armed forces, and more generally of what peace should entail. 130 Crisis Group interview, source from Lanao region, Manila, 8 May 2026. The military has tried to develop more flexible rules of engagement that allow for the immediate separation of warring parties, resorting to force if necessary. These guidelines, however, have not been applied consistently. Typically, the military manages to strike a ceasefire between the clashing parties, but as it does not have the mandate to resolve the issue that triggered the violence, the conflict often reignites further down the line. A vital element in these arrangements is often the payment of “blood money”, a form of compensation offered following an individual’s violent death. Some politicians, and even members of the MILF rank and file, have come to view this practice as harmful, since payment offers no guarantee that the conflict will cease. There are other obstacles to hammering out durable ceasefires. As conflicts tend to spill over village and town boundaries, a broader solution dealing with root causes in several municipalities, such as land ownership disputes, would be preferable. Municipal governments, however, often struggle to cooperate, which means this approach often is not feasible. 131 Crisis Group interview, former regional official, Cotabato City, 12 February 2026. In addition, regional ministries sometimes apply “ready made” solutions they have already successfully tested elsewhere, without taking into account the local context of the feud they are dealing with. 132 Crisis Group interview, MILF leaders, Maguindanao del Sur, 28 March 2026. This has occurred, for example, in Maguindanao. There were also cases where no ministerial intervention followed at all and local people resolved the conflict on their own. Even the MILF is not always able to resolve feuds beyond achieving a ceasefire. 133 In one case, a MILF commander around the MILF camp Abubakar hesitated to resolve a land issue between two of his followers and advised the village to take care of it. There was, however, no follow-up. Crisis Group interview, land experts, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Furthermore, a local non-governmental organisation noted that “infrequent and unstructured” peace dialogues most often fail to include women, young people with disabilities and non-Moro Indigenous people. 134 Moro Women Development and Cultural Center, Inc., “From Consultation to Action – Advancing Peace Together”, Summary Report, Peace Conference 2025, Davao City, 4 December 2025, p. 30. In some instances, this lack of inclusivity has perpetuated feuding or revived land conflicts that had otherwise been considered as resolved. V. Pathways to Local Stability Addressing the complexity of local conflict in the Bangsamoro cannot be done through a single sweeping reform. Rather, it requires a series of careful adjustments across institutions. 135 Crisis Group interviews, police, military and local Bangsamoro officials, January-March 2026. Focusing only on the police or the judiciary is unlikely to produce the desired results, which is why regional stability hinges on a combination of different policies. Police outpost in Cotabato City, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht A. Improving Security Coordination As the Bangsamoro stabilises, Manila has an opportunity to reorient its military toward external defence and set the foundation for the police to take the lead in managing day-to-day security in the region. While a full handover of responsibilities would be premature, the military and regional police can start formulating a plan to do so in the near future. 136 Crisis Group interview, police commission official, 12 February 2026. The existing Joint Peace and Security Coordinating Center (mentioned in Section IV.B) could be strengthened to take on this task. The centre should, for example, design more joint operations and establish a roadmap for regional and provincial security powers to be passed from the military to the police. Consolidating regional security will require a redistribution of state forces, while ensuring Mindanao retains a baseline military presence. 137 Crisis Group interviews, analysts, Manila, June-July 2024. The government should increase the police’s responsibilities in the region’s more stable areas, pairing this move with a gradual drawdown of military units. Mobile army platoons or detachments should deploy to volatile hotspots, including parts of Maguindanao del Sur, the mountainous corridor between Maguindanao and Lanao, and areas where non-Moro Indigenous communities live. To offset these small-unit redeployments, troops from the region’s flanks, such as the southern Visayas or eastern Mindanao, should shift to conflict-affected areas within the Bangsamoro in order to concentrate the military where it can maximise stability. Lastly, it is vital to deepen existing but modest military and police collaboration in Central Mindanao, through intelligence-sharing, joint training, and coordinated non-combat operations. 138 Crisis Group interview, senior military official, 16 February 2025. It is also crucial for the military to re-examine the rationale for auxiliary forces. In some areas that do not see conflict, some CAFGU paramilitary units should be demobilised. More broadly, better oversight of these forces is essential: commanders should apply strict accountability and disciplinary measures, and sanction transgressions. 139 Crisis Group interview, former military officer, Manila, 29 May 2024. In the long run, the Philippine government’s objective should be to dismantle all state-backed militias in a phased manner and rely only on professional forces. B. Reforming Regional Policing Reforming policing arrangements in a complex environment while remaining respectful of both the Philippine constitution and the Bangsamoro’s autonomous status will be difficult. As mentioned previously, Crisis Group takes the view that a Bangsamoro police force outside the realm of the national police is not practical at this stage. A more prudent approach in the short term is to reform the existing law enforcement set-up. 140 Crisis Group interviews, Lanao, Cotabato and Manila, February-March 2026. To that end, police stations must be resourced with the equipment they need. The national government should also hire more officers so as to boost the police-to-population ratio. Authorities could reassign qualified officers currently posted in peaceful areas outside the Bangsamoro to the region. They also could increase the recruitment of MILF and MNLF fighters into the regular police force, starting with those who passed the test but were never hired. Expanding the ranks of Moro officers would foster trust with both the MILF and with communities that still view the police with suspicion. Ensuring ex-rebel recruits receive proper training and mentoring, and are fully acquainted with the communities they serve, will be essential to prepare officers and cadets. Foreign donors involved with the peace process could support such initiatives with training design and funding. Adjustments in police operations could also help build a more credible force. Once it has the numbers and skills to do so effectively, the police should strengthen targeted deterrence in hotspots where clan feuds and community violence proliferate, combining surveillance, mediation and enforcement. It should also improve its intelligence gathering, including more information-sharing between police units and more efforts to question militants and individuals involved in feuding to understand the local drivers of conflict. Stepping up community policing would ... narrow the gap between police and the Bangsamoro public. Stepping up community policing would also narrow the gap between police and the Bangsamoro public. 141 Crisis Group interviews, police and regional government officials, Maguindanao and Lanao, February 2026. The regional police force should organise a new department that would recruit, train and deploy community safety officers. 142 Funding could come from the national or the regional budget, or a combination thereof. It should, however, bypass local governments and exclude their funding to prevent them from exerting undue influence. These would ideally be recruited among demobilised MILF rebels, and would be tasked with engaging local leaders and communities and conducting visible and non-confrontational patrols. They could also aid in criminal investigations. Before rolling this out across the Bangsamoro, Manila and the regional government could run a pilot project in some municipalities with independent monitoring of its progress. Here again, foreign donors could support such programs with targeted interventions. Lastly, to restore public trust, regional leaders should combat police corruption by enforcing existing regulations. The internal affairs service and other accountability bodies should reinforce such efforts through robust oversight. Tightening procurement and inventory controls is also essential to safeguard firearms and ammunition and prevent costly – and potentially dangerous – losses. C. Breaking Conflict Cycles Security reforms are vital, but quelling violence in the region will also require addressing longstanding conflicts. Regional and national authorities should strive to make local peace deals more durable and ensure stricter adherence to the rule of law. Curbing the proliferation of firearms will necessarily be part of that process. 1. Sustainable conflict resolution Tackling horizontal violence requires de-escalating tensions when they arise, preventing them from re-erupting, and addressing root causes through conflict resolution. To prevent local quarrels from morphing into full-blown firefights, security forces need to step in as early as possible. The army, police and MILF structures all have a role to play. While the military remains best equipped to quell firefights, particularly those involving clashing MILF (and possibly MNLF) factions, internal rifts within a single MILF unit are best mediated by the ex-rebels themselves. In case of minor incidents, relying on the mediation of trusted community figures would also help avoid escalation. Effective conflict resolution in the Bangsamoro should also reach beyond the rapid responses needed once violence breaks out to address the underlying causes of conflict. Initial ceasefire agreements should include clear protocols, including sanction mechanisms, laying out the next steps in case the conflict parties violate the terms of the agreement. Once ceasefires are in place, they require rigorous monitoring, whether through the deployment of nearby police and military units, or through the participation of informal community watchers – a mechanism that has already proved successful, for example last year in the case of some feuds in Datu Saudi Ampatuan and Mamasapano towns. 143 Crisis Group interviews, local mediators, Datu Saudi Ampatuan, Maguindanao del Sur, 28 March 2026. 2. Building inclusive justice The police may be the “first face of justice”, but the broader judicial sector needs to be reformed as well. 144 “Policing for the Bangsamoro”, op. cit., p. 18. A first task is to strengthen the courts. This should happen through better staffing and the provision of security guarantees for judges and prosecutors, particularly when it comes to accessing remote areas. Public Sharia courts also need more support, which could come in the form of training for MILF members who are currently judges in their respective communities, but wish to practice in public courts as counsellors. 145 Sharia counsellors are individuals who passed a Sharia legal exam administered by the Supreme Court. They can represent clients and practice law at public Sharia courts. Increasing the number of so-called “mobile courts” – whereby representatives of the judiciary visit far-flung areas where there are no tribunals – would also strengthen the standing of the judiciary. In the same spirit, the regional government should broaden access to the justice system for its most vulnerable citizens by subsidising legal fees and travel expenses for community members who need to go to court. 146 Crisis Group interview, legal official, Cotabato City, 5 August 2026. Encouraging state institutions to coordinate more closely with bodies engaging in customary practices such as community mediation would also increase the efficacy of the justice system. Courts and other institutions such as village justice systems can reap the benefit of these customary practices by formally recognising not just traditional mediators, but also the actual settlement agreements reached thanks to them. 3. Navigating the firearms conundrum Dealing with the proliferation of weapons is also imperative. To begin with, the government and the MILF should restart the decommissioning of firearms. Getting the MILF back onboard with this process requires the government to deliver the support it promised demobilised fighters in the 2014 peace accord. 147 The Annex on Normalisation stipulates that in exchange for disarmament, the national government will implement a variety of other measures including compensation for demobilised fighters and the economic development of MILF camps. Given the need for the government and the MILF to rebuild trust and overcome the current stalemate, a realistic timeline will require that the process continue after the September 2026 parliamentary elections. Beyond the MILF’s weapons, the government should address gun violence in Mindanao. That begins with getting a better picture of the number of firearms in circulation. In addition to credible estimates of guns in the hands of insurgents and ex-rebels, the military and police need updated inventories of firearms issued to police and military auxiliaries, as well as clear guidelines on the storage and safeguarding of their weapons so that leaks do not occur in the first place. The state should also disarm police or members of military auxiliaries who take part in conflicts or abuse their power, and dismiss them. For their part, national agencies must tighten controls on smuggling, imports and domestic manufacture of illegal guns, as well as strengthen oversight of gun licensing and weapon registration. Across all interventions, authorities should prioritise the confiscation of high-calibre firearms, given how lethal they can be. Deterring actual gun use is also critical. Establishing a highly visible and competent police presence should serve as the foundation for these efforts. To maximise impact, these police deployments ought to be combined with strict firearm bans across the region in the lead up to elections, when gun violence tends to peak. 148 The police said that until early August they arrested twelve persons for violating the gun ban. Joviland Rita, “PNP: 12 arrested for violating BARMM election gun ban”, GMA News , 3 August 2026. Authorities should also impose penalties not only on those who possess unlicensed firearms but also those who manufacture, store or use them for political ends. Religious leaders and clan elders can also contribute to eradicating the excesses of Bangsamoro’s gun culture by mounting campaigns to rectify the belief that the use of firearms beyond self-defence is legitimate. 149 Crisis Group interviews, local civil society, Cotabato and Marawi, February-March 2026. VI. Conclusion Armed rebellions have tailed off across the southern Philippines, but the peace they have given way to is constantly threatened by clan warfare, political volatility and factional disputes within the former insurgent MILF. The architects of the Bangsamoro peace agreement saw reforms to the police force, backed by improvements in institutions handling conflict resolution and justice, as a way to propel the region from war to peace. Yet a series of obstacles has slowed police reform and prevented institutions from maintaining law and order. Manila and the Bangsamoro government will need to work in tandem and be realistic about proposed reforms. A law enforcement system that is competent, representative and fair, and which can earn public trust by making communities safer, is an essential step forward. A more effective and accessible judicial system, as well as moves to tighten gun control and ensure that peacebuilding initiatives address the social and political undercurrent that lead to fighting, are also vital. These reforms would not only contain violence but also signal that the region’s institutions are catching up with its aspirations for peace. Somalia’s End-of-year Cliffhanger pzeiler Thu, 09/03/2026 - 16:47 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Podcast / Africa 03 September 2026 1 minutes Somalia’s End-of-year Cliffhanger This week on The Horn , Alan talks with Samira Gaid, founder and senior analyst at the Mogadishu-based think tank Balqiis, about the possible end of UNSOS, the UN logistics operation supporting African Union troops and Somali government forces fighting Al-Shabaab and what may come next. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Somalia In this episode of The Horn , Alan is joined by Samira Gaid, founder and senior analyst at the Mogadishu-based think tank Balqiis about the U.S. decision to oppose renewed United Nations logistical support for the 19-year-old African Union military mission in Somalia. Samira explains why UN logistical support has been critical to the AU mission as well as to Somali government forces fighting Al-Shabaab, and why its loss could leave some areas outside Mogadishu increasingly vulnerable. They also discuss what could happen if no solution or stopgap measure is found, and the 12,000-strong African Union mission ceases to function by the end of the year. They discuss how such a scenario could shift the balance of power on the battlefield between the federal government and Al-Shabaab. They also assess whether Mogadishu’s pursuit of bilateral security partnerships could fill the void left by a weakened or defunct AU mission. This episode is produced in partnership with the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung. Click here to listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify . For more, check out Balqiis’ report “ No Time to Drift: Somalia and the Deadline for a Managed Security Transition ” and our Somalia page.
